#7480. North Korean Ad Fraudsters Pwn Binance; Don’t Bother Predicting Your Ad Revenue

The ad industry has a long history of costly blunders – some absurd, some sinister – that have run into the millions.

Remember the night of the yellow square? Or, more troublingly, a recent rash of Google ad account takeovers?

If you hadn’t heard, Binance was totally pwned in a $6 billion crypto heist last week, suspected to be a North Korean operation. Well, Binance has now published what amounts to a preliminary autopsy report of the incident.

The heist began when a Binance Wallet DevOps team member accidentally downloaded a malicious copy of Homebrew – a popular open-source tool – from a mirror site promoted in a search ad. The malware was spotted, but not before the hackers had obtained the real identities of Wallet DevOps team members.

Using those identities, the North Korean hacking unit spent months targeting Binance’s wallet team with covert schemes. One involved a prolonged fake job interview that lured a Binance DevOps engineer into downloading an “assignment” onto their work device.

After taking control of the Binance DevOps engineer’s laptop, the hacker used an unnamed internal AI tool to log in to the devices of other engineers. Access to multiple credentials allowed the heist to go through.

A $6 billion reminder that one ad click can come at a staggering cost.

Publishers are contending with AI search eating into their traffic. But at The New York Times, the problem for investors wasn’t shrinking ad revenue; it was that growth isn’t happening fast enough for their liking.

The company reported on Wednesday that its Q3 digital ad revenue grew 12% to $109.9 million. Good stuff. But it slightly missed its own projection of growth in the “mid to high teens.”

Most publishers would kill for 12% growth right now. But it was the slowest digital ad growth rate the Times has posted since Q4 2024, when it grew by 9.5%.

Multiple investors pressed Times CEO Meredith Kopit Levien on the ad revenue miss. But, although she acknowledged in her opening remarks that the Times “isn’t immune” to “Big Tech companies whose moves continue to result in less traffic to publishers,” she didn’t directly answer questions about whether AI search contributed to the revenue shortfall. Instead, she kept reiterating that it’s hard to predict ad revenue quarter to quarter.

The NYT’s reluctance to directly address AI search contrasts with publishers like People Inc. and platforms like Reddit, which have been openly blasting Google for obliterating their search traffic.

Meanwhile, News Corp also reported earnings on Wednesday. The company’s Dow Jones division – which includes The Wall Street Journal, Barron’s, MarketWatch and more – also grew digital ad revenue by 12% last quarter. No investors pooh-pooh’d News Corp’s growth, though. One even offered his congratulations.

Guess that’s a lesson for publishers: These days, predicting your ad revenue may just be a liability.

Does opting out of being tracked by your smart TV actually work? According to new research from Northeastern University, not always, The Verge reports.

As part of the study, researchers analyzed network traffic from 12 different TV devices running eight operating systems, which included big players like LG, Amazon Fire, Google TV, Samsung, Roku, Vizio and VIDAA OS. They then checked which TVs had automatic content recognition (ACR) enabled by default and whether changing the sharing settings stopped those TVs from sending data.

Most TVs tracked viewing on their own built-in streaming services, but not on Netflix or YouTube. More than half also tracked content coming in through HDMI, such as from a cable box or game console. Opting out stopped the data flow on most devices – but Samsung and Roku TVs kept sending data from their own streaming services, while Walmart-owned Vizio TVs continued transmitting as before.

ACR is now table stakes for the smart TV industry, in part because it helps advertisers measure ad reach and frequency. But it’s also drawing more scrutiny – and opprobrium – from viewers who are only now realizing just how much of their viewing gets tracked.

The bots aren’t taking over just yet. Uber says it only fulfilled four rides and 500 food orders from third-party AI agents last quarter out of 320 million transactions. [The Verge]

#7475. DoorDash Just Bought The Ad Business It Couldn’t Build For Itself

Last week, the news became official: DoorDash acquired Instacart for $17 billion.

Earlier in the week, when the deal was still a well-sourced rumor, Needham, an investment bank, put out a note regarding the deal. Needham’s working theory was that the deal is about combining the two advertising businesses. Everything else is logistics.

So what does this deal actually mean for commerce media?

The easy read is that a delivery app is buying another delivery app. Actually, DoorDash is buying a revenue mix it has never managed to build for itself. Not for lack of trying. DoorDash bought ad-tech company Symbiosys for $175 million in 2025 to take its ads beyond its own app, and it has spent years pushing into grocery and retail.

Buying Instacart is DoorDash’s admission that building on its own wasn’t getting there fast enough.

Here is the arithmetic. Instacart’s advertising and other revenue was $297 million in the second quarter, 28.5% of everything it earned. Call it more than a quarter of the company. DoorDash passed a $1 billion run rate in ads two years ago and hasn’t broken the number out since. By my count, that’s around 10% of its revenue.

Both companies have billion-dollar ad businesses. Only one of them is an ad business.

That matters because delivery is a hard business and advertising is a highly profitable one. According to Wedbush, a financial securities firm, Instacart brings more than grocery drop-offs; it brings a marketplace across many grocers, plus an ad business brands pay to rank higher in search.

Delivery is low margin, and ads are high margin. Ads lift what the platform earns per order without charging the customer more. That is the beauty of a blended P&L.

How did Instacart end up setting the bar? It became an ads business because the grocers couldn’t deliver what they had promised brands.

Retail media was pitched as performance media for commerce. Ads at the point of conversion, closed loop, every dollar accounted for. What brands got from most grocers was run-of-site advertising with a sales report attached.

Some grocers built serious networks, such as Kroger Precision Marketing and Albertsons Media Collective. But even the good ones could only reach one retailer’s shoppers, and that left brands stitching together a dozen buys to cover a category.

Instacart could do something the grocers couldn’t. Because it sat on top of the last mile, it could bundle baskets and get hyper-specific across hundreds of retailers in one buy. A brand didn’t have to negotiate with Kroger, then Costco, then Publix. It bought the category once.

That’s the Uber model – a network of independent operators behind one front door – applied to grocery. (Not so coincidentally, Uber was also reportedly in the mix to acquire Instacart, but it backed out.)

Together, DoorDash and Instacart reach across occasions no one else covers in one place. DoorDash’s share of US delivery spending has grown from 44% to 59% over five years, while Instacart’s fell from 26% to 18%. Combined, a CPG brand could find the same household ordering dinner on DoorDash on Tuesday and groceries on Instacart on Saturday, across restaurants, grocery and convenience in a single buy.

But Instacart has differentiators that could prove to be worth its $17 billion price tag. Instacart is not reliant on individual grocery retailers, because it has direct relationships with consumers. Consumers opt in to sharing loyalty card data with Instacart for rewards at the grocer, and Instacart carries that opt-in. Plus, Instacart operates its own planogram model, so it decides how prominently it features products based on its own brand deals.

All of those factors make Instacart a true commerce media business. And Instacart’s direct relationships with consumers and brands can’t be easily disrupted by a grocer deciding to launch its own retail media platform.

Meanwhile, DoorDash built its relationships directly with restaurants. So Instacart’s relationships with grocers are truly additive.

Now, here’s the uncomfortable part: attribution.

Instacart nailed attribution on its own app. It has a 14-day window, basket-level reporting, a clean room since January and MRC accreditation for its impressions and clicks. What it never nailed is attribution to the retailer’s total sales, which is what the grocers promised in the first place.

Instacart sees the Instacart basket. Most grocery still happens in a store, and that halo is modeled, not measured. Brands kept spending anyway. They pay for the basket, not the proof. What is interesting is that the burden of proof shifted to the retailer rather than Instacart. Instacart can prove what happens in its own basket. So when a brand asks what its spend did in the store, the retailer is the one left without an answer.

There’s a bigger point here for commerce media. We’ve spent five years calling it an emerging channel, the thing on the test budget. It has just been priced as a scaled business asset, with closed-loop measurement on its own basket and modeling to show brands its impact in-store.

A public company just paid $17 billion, about a 30% premium, largely for an ad business built on shopper data. And the analysts covering the deal are valuing that ad business, not the drivers.

Commerce media is no longer just a line in the marketing plan; it is a line in the acquisition model.

#7473. Gamers Love Ad Blockers. So This Site Found Another Way To Show Them Ads

Ad blocking doesn’t just prevent publishers from earning revenue; it also creates blind spots in their audience analytics that can affect everything from monetization strategy to editorial coverage.

Gamers are very likely to use ad blockers, which has led to significant challenges for WiseGuyGaming, a video game-focused publication that launched last year.

Its co-founder and CEO, Mike Smith, launched the publication with his son Mikhail following previous stints handling audience data and monetization for HBO, Forbes and Hearst. After two-plus decades working at established media brands, he wanted to start his own, he told AdExchanger.

However, the elder Smith quickly realized that the audience he most wanted to reach – technologically sophisticated gamers – are disproportionately likely to use the most advanced ad blockers on the market. Those ad blockers made this audience largely invisible to existing analytics solutions, in addition to being unreachable with banner and video ads.

As a result, WiseGuyGaming found that about 18% of its audience used ad-blocking tech. Now it’s strategizing how to reach that audience in ways that can’t be blocked as easily as a web banner.

In addition to the Google Analytics tools widely used by publishers, WiseGuyGaming also relies on another popular third-party audience analytics and bot filtration tool, FouAnalytics, to measure its audience.

It’s especially important for publishers to use multiple analytics solutions these days, Marti said, because an explosion in bot-crawling activity to support generative and agentic AI has made it harder to separate human site visitors from bots.

Plus, Marti said, there are now more services like Bright Data that turn consumer devices like cellphones and TVs into residential proxies for AI scraping and other bot activity.

Basically, if an app installed on a person’s TV partners with Bright Data, that person can opt in to allow their IP address to be used to mask bot behavior. In exchange, they get an ad-free experience when using the app or some other incentive.

These proxy services make it harder for publishers to weed out bots using traditional methods like blocking IP addresses associated with previous bot activity, Marti said. Proxy services can make a bot appear to be using a residential IP address, rather than one tied to a data center.

However, there are nuances in how bot crawlers work when they load a publisher page that can be exploited to detect them, Marti said.

For instance, he said, many crawlers are configured to scrape a website’s data before any third-party scripts – including ad tech and bot-blocking tech – are able to execute on the page.

“The crawling company has been told, ‘Go to this page and [extract] the content of the big table on that page as JSON,’” Marti said. “The crawler is smart enough to know that all the social widgets on the page, all the random third-party JavaScript, ads, analytics – it doesn’t need that for the mission it’s on.” The crawler’s headless browser often doesn’t even bother sending the network requests required for the third-party scripts to run, he said.

But, as it turns out, Marti added, ad blockers likewise prevent the browser from sending network requests to ping third-party scripts, including ad tech and analytics. Which means publishers can use more advanced bot-detection strategies to also reveal when a human site visitor is using an ad blocker.

When a user with an ad blocker arrives on the page, the ad blocker references lists of known third-party ad servers and domains associated with ad tech, then prevents network requests from pinging those servers and domains.

Marti and Smith’s solution was to set up two versions of FouAnalytics on the WiseGuyGaming site.

But the other version used a “proxy pass” – or a first-party URL – to obscure the third-party script, he said. “It’s on wiseguygaming.com, so it’s not going to show up on any of the filter lists. But it is proxied through to the same FouAnalytics server as the third-party script, so we’ve got the exact same script being served onto the page twice.”

WiseGuyGaming could then compare data between its two different FouAnalytics dashboards to see which users were blocking the FouAnalytics third-party script, but not blocking FouAnalytics when it was using the proxy pass.

And since both Google Analytics and FouAnalytics had already prefiltered out likely bots, WiseGuyGaming could conclude with reasonable certainty that the remaining 18% still blocking FouAnalytics as a third-party script were probably either invalid traffic that evaded the bot filter or humans using an ad blocker.

Once WiseGuyGaming nailed down that roughly 18% figure for its ad-blocking audience, it then had to come up with a new way to reach those users, since banner ads wouldn’t cut it.

WiseGuyGaming’s immediate solution was to produce more sponsored and native content, which ad blockers are not configured to recognize, Smith said.

Meanwhile, the site’s editorial team was able to analyze the ad-blocking audience’s traffic patterns to understand what content was resonating with them, Smith said. Which is helping the editors to publish more content that can bring in that highly technical audience the Smiths want to reach.

The solution did have one flaw, Marti noted. It required them to look at two different FouAnalytics dashboards in two different browser tabs to compare the ad-blocking and non-ad-blocking audiences.

But that’s a minor concern, since the solution has transformed WiseGuyGaming’s editorial and monetization strategies, Smith said.

“We set out first to get a very pure count of our audience,” he said. “We are now going to launch a paid subscription service and use email and push [notification] technology to reach the roughly 18% that we found.”

#7471. Reddit tests new search ads

In a blog post published on November 3, Reddit revealed that it’s testing a new ad product. Alongside a “select group of eligible advertisers,” the social platform is experimenting with paid media posts that show up in its search results.

The new ads will harness Reddit’s “existing ad targeting” to surface relevant product recommendations on search pages. The blog post provided two examples of how that process could work: A search for “espresso station” could show results for coffee machines, beans, and mugs, and a query for “home office equipment” could deliver paid listings for monitors, desks, and chairs.

The search ads have plenty of utility for brands that want to reach Reddit’s growing community, which includes a large share of Millennial and Gen Z users. A few years ago, Reddit was cited as the fastest-growing social media site, and its ascendance as a search hub is a big part of that story. As Google stuff its results with AI Overviews, Reddit still delivers answers that are written by humans.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Search ads will turn that competitive advantage into an asset for brands. The new format is part of a broader effort to promote Reddit content while it’s still on Reddit. The platform’s greatest hits often go viral on other platforms, where those posts are sometimes paired with unrelated videos. To keep more traffic in house, Reddit has rolled out a new video product that resembles TikTok.

Paid media in search results promotes Reddit’s homegrown community, but in other areas, the ads will be unable to help Reddit grow its position in the search game. The role of generative AI chatbots in that industry has become a major topic of discussion. Large language models (LLMs) scrape social platforms and use those data points to response to search queries.

Reddit was once the king of chatbot referrals; that advantage inspired other platforms to copy its signature layout. YouTube has since snatched the chatbot referral crown from Reddit.

The LLMs, however, scrape creator content rather than ads. So while Reddit is turning its results pages into an opportunity for brands, those advertisers will still have to link up with creators if they want to meddle with chatbot-based searches.

#7465. Netflix might want its new AI search to drum up more “quality” viewership

Netflix‘s new strategy for combating YouTube‘s commanding share of living room TVs is to insist that it’s not the quantity of viewership, but the quality.

And it might be trying to pump up those quality views with a new recommendation tool.

Of course, the times being what they are, the tool is AI.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

AI Discover is intended to curate Netflix’s offerings in a hyperpersonalized manner, so people only see what they like. If this sounds familiar, it’s because Netflix is doing what YouTube, X, and Meta have already done: shunt the responsibility for a quality recommendation algorithm onto viewers and their input.

“There’s more to enjoy and discover on Netflix than ever, but what sounds right for a quiet night in may look different for family movie night or a few spare minutes,” Netflix said in an announcement post. “We’ve spent years refining how you discover, with recommendations tailored to your tastes, from what you Thumbs Up to what you add to ‘My List.’ Now, AI Discover joins the mix as a new way to explore.”

Once a theme is in place, Netflix’s bot brings up a bunch of suggestions, and also additional narrower themes within the first themes. Netflix says there will be a process of “tuning” AI Discover’s recommendations until it “find[s] your next obsession.”

Users who think the bot is getting too far off what they want can refresh the whole deal. Netflix also lets people tell it titles they don’t like.

Unlike the aforementioned social media platforms, Netflix doesn’t seem to have included a ChatGPT-esque discussion aspect to this tool. Users just click through and select what they like, and what they don’t.

Makes sense, since YouTube, Meta, and X have their own in-house chatbots they can shove into everything; Netflix doesn’t have a Gemini or Grok or Muse equivalent, so a yes/no system is its best option. It did partner with OpenAI in 2025 to test an AI search feature that was rumored would replace its regular search function, but that never materialized in full across the service. Maybe this is the version of that idea it ultimately ended up with, sans GPT chatting.

Netflix does say AI Discover is “powered by a new intelligence layer we’ve been building that responds to what members tell us in real time and keeps learning.”

This brings us back to what we said at the top of this article: Netflix is looking for quality viewership. And, well, if it can gather an immense amount of information about viewers’ preferences with this new “intelligence layer,” it might be able to more accurately match them with what they want to watch.

That in turn could drive up the amount of time people spend watching a movie or a TV show–and Netflix might start shooting for average view duration as a way to supercede YouTube.

For now, Netflix’s new AI discovery is only available on TVs in the U.S. (interesting choice), and only in English. Netflix says it won’t appear on kids’ profiles. Per Variety, the streamer plans to expand to more international users in the coming weeks.

#7463. Ads Drive Consumer Demand. The Shelf Captures It

Imagine you’re shopping for laundry detergent. You click to buy your preferred brand, but when your order is fulfilled, the product is out of stock. What do you do?

Recent DoorDash data shows that shoppers in this scenario buy a competing brand nearly 12% of the time, while more than 40% of the time they request a refund instead. In either case, the preferred brand just lost an easy opportunity to convert on strong demand.

This isn’t a niche problem. Inventory distortion from out-of-stocks and overstocks costs the retail industry an estimated $1.7 trillion each year, according to IHL Group. That makes capturing that demand a huge growth opportunity for brands.

The challenge here is that most commerce media platforms are great at measuring advertising performance but don’t fully understand the conditions under which advertising is trying to convert. That missing context is becoming increasingly consequential as brands invest more heavily in commerce media.

Commerce media’s greatest strength is proximity to the transaction. Advertisers can connect media exposure to purchases and measure impact against verified sales.

But many other factors can derail conversion. A product might be missing from the retailer’s digital assortment, or the listing might lack a title, image or product detail to give the shopper confidence. In each case, the brand doesn’t have a full view of the lost opportunity.

Conventional advertising metrics can tell us what happened (click/no click, sale/no sale, etc.), but often lack the context to explain why or why not, as the case may be. And if marketers don’t understand why something happened, it’s easy to optimize for the wrong variable.

When a campaign delivers strong engagement but disappointing sales or category share, the natural response is to adjust the media strategy by changing the targeting or creative or shifting spending toward other products or retailers. But what if the campaign was reaching the right consumers and generating genuine purchase intent only to encounter one of the availability problems discussed above?

In that case, shifting budget away from the “underperforming” product or retailer actually means walking away from demonstrated consumer demand.

The same applies to substitution behavior. When shoppers can’t get their preferred product, do they choose another product within the brand’s portfolio, switch to a competitor or abandon the purchase altogether?

Each of those actions merits a distinct strategic response. A product that consistently loses shoppers to competitors during stockouts might warrant greater attention from sales and supply-chain teams. A product with strong demand but poor digital visibility might need better catalog execution to maximize advertising outcomes.

The takeaway is that advertising amplifies demand and content drives conversion – but growth is delivered on the shelf. And without visibility into that full order journey, it’s easy to pour money into fixing a problem that doesn’t exist.

These gaps in contextual understanding stem from a familiar problem in ad tech: fragmented workflows and siloed data. Marketing teams manage campaign strategy, delivery and performance. Ecommerce oversees product listings and content. Sales and category teams manage retailer relationships and assortment. Supply-chain teams focus on inventory and availability.

Organizations haven’t connected the data in a way that helps them understand if and where demand hits a snag along the buying journey. For decades, point of sale and syndicated sales data has helped CPGs understand what sold in stores. But sales data alone rarely explains why a product didn’t sell. Was it out of stock? Was the shopper’s preferred item or size unavailable? Did they choose another product or switch to a competitor when at the shelf?

But even when brands have inventory data, they can’t always keep up with what shoppers encounter. Shelves change by the hour and any data source – whether it’s a brand’s, a retailer’s or a periodic audit – is just a snapshot.

Newer approaches are helping close that gap by connecting advertising data with real-world commerce signals. At DoorDash, for example, we’re evolving Ads Manager into Brand Center, bringing advertising performance together with on-shelf availability, assortment insights and consumer purchasing insights. By combining order data with in-store signals captured by Dashers, brands can see not only where sales are happening, but where demand may be going unfulfilled due to out-of-stocks and what shoppers choose instead when a product isn’t available.

This integrated visibility is helping different teams within an organization work from a shared understanding of what’s constraining growth so they can figure out who can actually do something about it.

Commerce media has rapidly become a core marketing channel because of how it’s made advertising more measurable and more optimizable. But to mature further, commerce media performance needs to be connected with the broader commercial context that determines whether demand becomes revenue.

That deeper contextual visibility brings a new set of questions that lead to critical insights, including, “Which products are generating demand that isn’t being fulfilled?” and “Where are availability or assortment gaps suppressing sales?”

Marketers don’t have to become inventory managers or supply-chain experts. But they should have enough visibility to recognize when a disappointing campaign result isn’t actually an advertising problem. Because a commerce media program with impressive advertising metrics isn’t worth much if it’s not driving real revenue.

Sometimes, the best way to improve advertising performance has nothing to do with the ad itself.

High-end ad blockers mimic some of the same behavior as bot traffic. So WiseGuyGaming repurposed the tools it was already using to identify bots to reveal its ad-blocking audience as well.

AppLovin is growing at a blistering pace, but Wall Street investors remain cautious about the business.

The mobile ad tech company earned just shy of $2.2 billion in Q3 this year, per the company’s earnings report after-hours on Wednesday. Of that, $1.44 billion fell straight to net income (which is to say, profit). That is an “industry-leading” profit margin of about 66%, said CFO Matthew Stumpf.

It’s the type of number ad tech companies haven’t seen since Rocket Fuel hit the market. Which, admittedly, isn’t such fantastic company, considering Rocket Fuel’s disastrous downfall. But that association – not with Rocket Fuel, but with third-party ad tech – is part of the challenge for AppLovin.

Co-Founder and CEO Adam Foroughi addressed the education and mind-shifting among media buyers (and, ahem, among its investors) that needs to happen for its consumer ad business to accelerate.

“People have to go, ‘This is a bigger ad tech company, that’s sort-of-independent ad tech without a first-party site, [and] bigger than anything we’ve ever seen before,’” Foroughi told investors.

There is a great deal of “headroom for growth,” as Foroughi put it multiple times throughout the call, when it comes to the consumer ad business. But filling that headroom is going to take a lot of time.

Right now, AppLovin’s consumer ads segment is growing fast – more than 100% year over year, Foroughi said, though revenue for that segment is not disclosed. That business was only formally launched out of beta last year, so the revenue is still relatively low. The business will compound over time, he said, as advertisers figure out the platform and run incrementality attribution studies to feel confident with the ROAS.

Foroughi pointed to the changes Apple is making to iOS and mobile web inventory as another reason for advertisers to get on board with AppLovin’s platform.

“A lot of what’s called, I guess, traditionally, ‘open web,’” Foroughi said, is actually just a cheap reach play. That mentality is not like AppLovin’s ad system, which tracks and values impressions through to the point of conversion, he said. A healthy platform with strong ROAS may very well see CPM increases, despite being antithetical to the cheap reach mindset. But the mobile gaming space is “much, much bigger” now, he added, and the web is becoming less trackable.

“We think a lot of those dollars will shift into the app space,” he said.

Then there’s AppLovin’s creative knowledge gap.

Advertisers in the consumer segment have mostly not purchased ads in mobile games before, nor are they familiar with the particulars of how AppLovin’s media platform works, according to Fouroughi.  Mobile game advertisers all use the platform already, and they have specific creative that, say, offers a mini-game or test gameplay to prompt a download. Ecommerce advertisers on social media can’t just port over their creatives.

For one thing, he said that social platforms are all about super-quick videos with a hook delivered in a second or two. But AppLovin’s gaming audience is watching a full-screen ad for 30-60 seconds. It practically never happens on a social feed.

“There’s a learning process here that has to happen so that the media buyers really understand the framework,” Foroughi said.

Eventually, agencies and advertisers will figure it out and approach AppLovin as an always-on platform with a standardized approach to creative.

“There will be playbooks for our platform,” he prophesied.

AppLovin laid out an ambitious marker on its earnings call.

“We believe this business can compound at roughly 30% annually over the long term,” Foroughi said of the ad tech business.

The current earnings report has ad revenue up by 55% and a profit margin that, as Foroughi put it, “is probably second to none.”

But 30% growth over the long term is bold, considering the multibillion-dollar scale of AppLovin’s ad business. And investors are still wary.

Some advertisers purportedly anticipate price hikes on AppLovin, since there are now gaming and consumer advertisers bidding for the same impressions, Stephen Ju of UBS Investment Bank noted.

Matthew Cost of Morgan Stanley wondered when the “law of large numbers” would catch up with AppLovin, and the company could no longer project 20%-30% growth. He also asked Foroughi whether the headroom he promised would come from CTV. Foroughi didn’t think AppLovin would see “accretive” numbers on CTV anytime soon. But there is a pilot program running right now for AppLovin CTV ads.

Shweta Khajuria, of Wolfe Research, put it most directly: “As an ad tech company for investors who are questioning the visibility of your business model and how much confidence you have in the durability of your top-line growth, is there something else incremental that you would consider sharing that would give more confidence in terms of the way your product works?”

For one thing, Foroughi said, AppLovin has delivered strong earnings that exceed investor expectations in 15 of the past 16 quarterly reports. No other large public tech company has its combination of scale, growth rate and profit margin.

Still, the consumer business is too nascent to offer confident predictive benchmarks around its growth or revenue totals, he said. “You sort of have to make your own guesses.”

AppLovin’s earnings can’t just be hand-waved away, nor is its margin vulnerable to any sudden collapse, as happened when Rocket Fuel disclosed a take rate above 60%.

AppLovin is an actual economic force in the mobile economy.

“That ad spend is creating GDP,” Foroughi said. “It’s creating new transactions that otherwise wouldn’t have been there.”

#7458. Some students watch thousands of irrelevant videos during class. Can YouTube solve that problem?

Platforms like YouTube have become ubiquitous in classrooms. A recent report from Gallup found that 96% of students are equipped with devices that are meant to enhance their learning.

Reality, however, is not so straightforward. Some students are using their devices to watch videos that don’t qualify as educational. In the most extreme cases, kids and teens watch thousands of those videos each semester; with those behaviors, classroom devices become distractions, not academic aids.

That was one conclusion NBC News drew after surveying student YouTube habits over an entire academic year. The study was not broad — only 11 kids and their parents turned over classroom viewership records — but it was deep. NBC News analyzed more than 17,000 videos and uncovered some concerning trends.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

One Wisconsin sixth grader viewed more than 2,200 videos during the school year, but only 21 were deemed educational. An eighth grader in Pennsylvania watched a whopping 4,700 videos over the same period, and only a small fraction suited the intended use of his classroom device. Those findings echo a recent report published by the Wall Street Journal. That article told the story of a student who watched 13,000 videos on a school-issued device over three months.

To be clear, not all of the students in the NBC News sample are misusing their school devices. Four members of the 11-person cohort mostly used YouTube as intended by viewing educational videos while at school. Around the same time the WSJ report came out, software company Securly tracked classroom traffic and concluded that most students are only on YouTube for about five minutes of the school day.

The educators cited in the NBC News report, however, believe that any kids who are misusing YouTube in the classroom must receive help. “Even if this is just 1% of students, it’s still troubling that this is happening,” BYU Associate Communications Professor Scott Haden Church told NBC News. “It’s something that needs to be understood and regulated.”

As a counterargument, YouTube can claim that it does offer various forms of regulation. Its Player for Education is meant to deliver a distraction-free viewing environment that can keep students from getting off track.

“Our tools allow administrators to block the platform entirely or restrict access to teacher-assigned videos only, with no ads, recommendations, or browsing,” said Google spokesperson Jack Malon in a statement provided to NBC News. “If schools choose to enable browsing for students, we require them to get permission from parents first.”

YouTube itself looks to be taking a different approach. It is working with creators like Mark Rober to develop video-based curricula, and channels like Veritasium have delivered interactive learning experiences to the gaming hub known as Playables.

At this point, YouTube’s presence in classrooms may be inevitable, even if stronger rules are put into place. In that environment, adding positive resources to the platform can help students get the most out of their classroom devices.

#7455. Agencies Are Not Pitch Perfect; Magnite (And Everyone Else) Bets On Agentic

WPP CEO Cindy Rose recently criticized the rise of “CEO handshake” account wins, which is when an agency skips the pitch but still lands the account through an apparent CEO-to-CEO deal that bypasses the CMO.

“I do not think we do ourselves any favor as an industry of professionals by encouraging clients to bypass proper due diligence,” she told investors last week.

Rose didn’t specifically name Publicis in her references to CEO handshakes, though the holdco’s recent account wins fit the pattern. Publicis landed PepsiCo without pitching, following similar wins for Microsoft in April and LVMH’s APAC account in September.

Publicis, for its part, rejected the characterization in an open letter to Rose, published by Adweek. It begins, “Dear Cindy,” and continues: “Claiming we win on a ‘CEO handshake’ is an insult to clients’ intelligence.”

The letter goes on to note that clients “would never have entrusted us with a task of this magnitude on a wink and a handshake.”

Well, whatever the label, Publicis now owns these accounts and will be accountable if the work falls short.

Happy Daylight Savings and quarterly earnings season.

Magnite, which reported earlier this week, saw a 14% year-over-year revenue increase to $204.2 million in Q3. Connected TV was a highlight (no surprises there), with CTV revenue jumping 39% YOY. CTV has steadily grown as a share of Magnite’s business and now accounts for 53% of the total.

What’s new this quarter, however, is the role of agentic AI. Agentic workflows are infiltrating modern media buying, including for CTV. Agentic media buys can include formats that aren’t yet standardized for programmatic. Think home-screen ads, pause ads and smart TV tiles.

Which is why, during its earnings call, Magnite execs touted how the company is using agentic workflows to sell LG TV home screen inventory.

Magnite is also optimistic about SpringServe, which is not just an ad server, thank you very much. SpringServe is being pitched as a programmatic and mediation platform, a role that helps position Magnite as “the operating system for CTV monetization,” CEO Michael Barrett told investors.

That strategy could pay off as more ad decisioning shifts over to the sell side.

ChatGPT ads are generating less revenue per session than Google Search ads, early data suggests.

Digiday reports that the average is $0.89 for ChatGPT, compared with $2.45 for Google, citing a paper by Maximilian Kaiser and Christian Schulze that is still under review.

One possible reason is limited ad reach. Similarweb and Graphite data show that even in the UK, the market with the highest rate, ads reach just under 46% of eligible ChatGPT users.

And even among users who have seen ads, there’s no set frequency. According to OpenAI, ads appear only when they’re considered additive and relevant to the conversation and never in conversations about sensitive topics.

Yet even with those guardrails, some ads appear to be missing the mark. Paid ChatGPT traffic has a 0.37% conversion rate, compared with 1.17% for Google.

#7454. Stream, meet sea: Carnival is integrating Twitch into its cruises

When Dolly Parton and Kenny Rogers sang about “Islands in the Stream,” I don’t think they were talking about Twitch, but Carnival Cruise Line has other ideas. The Florida-based travel company will stream on the open seas with Play Carnival, an initiative that will show viewers how much fun they can have aboard the Celebration ship.

Play Carnival will kick off on November 15 on the cruise line’s official Twitch account. Carnival Fleet Cruise Director Erin Weigand will be joined by veteran creator iJustine, who will become a “player” as she takes on various challenges aboard Celebration.

The stream will include interactive elements thanks to the participation of Twitch chat. Viewers will decide iJustine’s fate by choosing her destinations aboard the ship and steering her toward various quests.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Destinations in Carnival’s Paradise Collection will also be highlighted. The goal is to keep a “fun meter” from hitting zero. With that branding, Play Carnival ties into the company’s “Find Your Fun Again” campaign.

“We’re constantly looking for new ways to push the boundaries on how we connect with consumers, and Play Carnival takes that thinking to a whole new level,” said Carnival VP of Brand, Product, and Social Media Michael Sotelo in a statement. “Through our ‘Carnival Is Calling’ campaign, we’re inviting people to discover the fun of a Carnival vacation, and Play Carnival brings that invitation to a new audience in an entirely new way. We’re excited to bring the worlds of gaming and cruising together, partnering with iJustine to make it happen.”

The cruise industry has rebounded since its COVID-era nadir, and Gen Z travelers have been a big reason why. Zoomers have consistently identified their desire for unique experiences over traditional travel destinations, and creator-led cruises can certainly bring excitement to vacations that might otherwise be run-of-the-mill. In 2022, Dude Perfect set sail aboard the Norwegian Pearl, and the social-savvy Snake Discovery zoo made a similar move in 2025.

Other creator cruises, however, have reminded us that the waters aren’t always calm. Gamer Northernlion announced an “ultimate streamer cruise” earlier this year, but the trip was ultimately cancelled.

By leveraging more than 50 years of experience, Carnival can ensure that its Twitch stream goes off without a hitch. iJustine might have to play hard to keep the fun meter alive, but on a cruise, that won’t be too difficult.

#7446. TikTok Shop now has a standalone app in four Southeast Asian markets

According to one estimate, the ecommerce market in Southeast Asia will generate $226 billion of gross merchandise value in 2026. TikTok Shop already accounts for a sizable chunk of that GMV, but ByteDance‘s ecommerce hub is looking to increase the size of its market share. With the launch of a standalone Shop app, TikTok will position itself to compete more directly with retailers like Shein and Temu.

Android and iOS versions of the standalone TikTok Shop app have arrived in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and The Philippines. The app was launched with little fanfare, but was spotted by tech consultant Matt Navarra.

With free shipping offers and app-exclusive deals, TikTok is trying to get Southeast Asian consumers to make purchases directly through the new Shop hub. A secure payments platform is also incorporated into the app.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Southeast Asia has long been the backbone of TikTok’s business. By 2022, that region had already delivered more than one trillion TikTok views. With that cultural movement, TikTok usurped traditional streaming services and built the foundation of its ecommerce push.

As TikTok Shop has traveled west, regions like the U.S. have accounted for a greater portion of the platform’s GMV. To capitalize on American spending power, TikTok has announced several partnerships and integrations that will get its Shop ready for the 2026 holiday rush.

It wouldn’t be fair to suggest that TikTok Shop has abandoned its Asian base, but rival platforms have sensed an opportunity to ramp up their activity in Eastern markets. YouTube, for example, has announced a partnership with AliExpress that unites it with one of China’s most prominent retailers.

If the standalone Shop app convinces more consumers to make their purchases directly through TikTok, an international expansion would be a logical next step. That is, however, a big ask — popular ecommerce platforms like Shopee are unlikely to surrender their customers without a fight.

#7440. YouTube’s biggest creators join forces to support the Susan Wojcicki Foundation’s critical mission: changing the conversation about lung cancer

In August 2024, YouTube‘s former longtime CEO, Susan Wojcicki, passed away at age 56. She battled non-small-cell lung cancer for two years and left behind one heck of a legacy.

Now Susan’s husband Dennis Troper and her sisters, Dr. Janet Wojcicki and Anne Wojcicki, have teamed up with professionals in clinical research, AI, diagnostics, and early detection to launch the Susan Wojcicki Foundation, which wants to “change the conversation” around lung cancer and help more people access screening, early detection, and prevention.

And, fittingly, the SWF is marking Lung Cancer Awareness Month by telling people about its mission on YouTube–with the help of creators.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

MrBeast, Mark Rober, Hank Green, Lilly Singh, Cassey Ho, Marina Mogilko, Cleo Abram, Mark Vins, Jake Roper, sWooZie, Matthew & Stephanie Patrick, Dr. Mike, Stephanie Chuang, and Rhett & Link all joined the SWF’s first YouTube video, offering their advice about how it can most effectively connect with viewers and share its message.

“The channel and its contents will address the fact that anyone with lungs can get lung cancer, and nobody deserves it,” Audrey Eatherly, the SWF’s Head of Creator and Community Partnerships, tells Tubefilter. “Early detection and prevention are key. But stigma and confusion keep too many people from talking about it or asking about a screening.”

The widespread assumption that only smokers can get lung cancer and the societal propensity to blame people who get it is a critical challenge to helping them, she adds. Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer deaths worldwide, killing more people each year than leukemia, lymphoma, and breast and prostate cancers combined.

“And yet, it receives the least amount of funding per death,” she says. “The stigma and misunderstanding have been barriers to addressing this critical challenge.”

Yvonne Diaz, a co-founder & Chair @ Oncogene Cancer Research and Board Member @ ALK Positive who has stage 4 ALK+ lung cancer, puts it well: “No matter how you wound up with lung cancer, you deserve the best outcomes, the best care, the best support, and empathy.”

Eatherly says the SWF wanted to bring its mission home to YouTube because the platform has the power to “transform lung cancer research into meaningful human conversations, bringing experts, research, real stories, shared experiences, and understanding to the forefront.”

The channel will share “credible, science-backed information and recent advancements” through things like deep-dive interviews with experts, informative Shorts, FAQs, and creator collaborations, she says.

Speaking of creators, they aren’t just helping launch the SWF’s YouTube channel. Jake Roper, Mark Vins (aka Brave Wilderness), sWooZie, and Matthew & Stephanie Patrick are all on the foundation’s official Creator Advisory Council.

“As longtime creators on YouTube, Matthew and I recognize the massive impact the platform has had on the world and how Susan Wojcicki’s leadership shaped its growth for almost a decade,” the Patricks tell Tubefilter. “The Susan Wojcicki Foundation carries Susan’s legacy forward through the very platform she helped build, and the creators whose careers she made possible are here to help spread its message. While YouTube is an entertainment platform, for many people it’s also their primary source of information and education online, making it a powerful place for the Susan Wojcicki Foundation to share a global message about lung cancer awareness and treatment.”

Stephanie also notes that she has a master’s degree in cancer pharmacology, and has seen firsthand “the massive scientific advancements made in the last decade in cancers that were previously thought to be untreatable.”

“The research the Susan Wojcicki Foundation is supporting is incredibly promising and could lead to significant improvements in patient outcomes while accelerating progress in lung cancer care,” she says.

Vins adds that he’s dedicated to the SWF because he wants to honor Susan’s lasting presence in the creator space.

“Susan was revered as a business leader who helped shape the technology and media landscape, but to creators, she was revered for something even more personal—her unwavering belief in our potential,” he says. “She empowered our voices at a time when the possibilities of YouTube were only beginning to emerge. She understood that creators weren’t simply making videos, we were building communities and creating relationships that would make a meaningful impact in the world.

“Ultimately, the greatest way I can honor Susan’s legacy is to do exactly what she always encouraged us to do: speak from the heart, create with integrity, and use our platforms to make a positive difference. Susan believed in the power of creators to change the world. I hope we can continue proving her right to bring greater awareness to lung cancer and support the pursuit of early detection that will save lives.”

You can check out the SWF’s YouTube channel here, and read more about its mission on its website.

#7437. Google, TikTok, and Meta are suing California to stop a law that bans “psychologically exploitative features” for kids under 16

Google, TikTok, and Meta have each filed suit against California in an attempt to block enforcement of a law that protects kids under 16 from “psychologically exploitative features” on social media platforms.

Governor Gavin Newsom signed the law, Assembly Bill 1709, into law this past September. “We want our children–and every California ​kid–to grow up in a world where technology supports their wellbeing, rather than exploits their vulnerabilities,” Newsom said at the time.

AB 1709 prevents socmed platforms from being able to employ features like recommendation algorithms, infinite scroll, and video autoplay on accounts of users under the age of 16. Because of how Google, TikTok, and Meta have designed their platforms, it effectively bans kids under 16 from having accounts at all on YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, and Facebook.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

According to Reuters, the three big tech companies all said (in separate lawsuits) that California is wrongly forcing them to use a state-mandated method of delivering content to children, instead of leaving things up to parents’ discretion.

Their lawsuits claim violations of Section 230 (aka the “safe harbor” law that lets platforms off the liability hook for anything their users post) and First Amendment free speech protections.

“Parents ‌are best ⁠positioned to make the right decisions for their families,” Google spokesperson Jose Castaneda told Reuters. “Overly broad laws like this actually break the systems we’ve built to help kids find high-quality, age-appropriate videos.”

In its suit, TikTok said protected speech “cannot be suppressed solely to protect the young from ideas or images that a legislative body thinks is unsuitable.”

Meta’s suit, meanwhile, said California doesn’t have the right to override its editorial standards.

“We are challenging this law because it violates the First Amendment by letting the government dictate how ideas are organized, displayed or shared with Californians,” a Meta spokesperson told Courthouse News. “Under the law, we would be forced to either remove features that keep teens’ experiences age-appropriate, or cut thousands of California teens off from family, friends and their communities.”

TikTok’s suit said ​protected speech “cannot be suppressed solely to ​protect the young from ideas ⁠or images that a legislative body thinks unsuitable.”

“AB 1709 is a blatantly unconstitutional restriction on free expression that erodes the long-standing and protected practice of curating content based on user preferences, which book stores, TV networks and streaming services all use,” a TikTok spokesperson added. “Beyond disregarding real progress in making teens safer online, this law limits free speech and takes away parents’ rights to determine what’s appropriate for their kids.”

The defendant in all three suits is California Attorney General Rob Bonta; all three suits ask the court for an injunction that would stop him from enforcing AB 1709 against them.

Bonta’s office said it’s reviewing the suits, and that he is “committed to defending California’s commonsense laws to protect kids online.”

Discover effective strategies to generate demand and measure results for your B2B marketing campaigns successfully.

Adding another B2B marketing channel only helps if your team can capture the interest it creates and evaluate whether that investment is working. A promising traffic report is not the same as evidence that a campaign generated additional demand.

In How To Create Demand You Can Actually Convert (And Prove), Shaun Bruno, Senior Growth Marketing Manager at CallRail, and Colin Saunders of Matter Made explained how they approached channel selection, secured funding for tests, and measured results before scaling spend.

Bruno described how CallRail simplified its marketing mix around paid search and the landing pages needed to convert existing demand. The team then strengthened measurement, clarified its ideal customer profile, and built out consideration and retargeting programs before investing further in awareness.

That sequence mattered more than copying CallRail’s full channel mix. As Shaun Bruno put it:

“But the important takeaway is that you don’t need to run all these channels.”

His broader point was that the bottom of the funnel needed to support the demand created at the top. More reach would not repair a landing page, offer, or follow-up process that failed to convert interested buyers.

Saunders distinguished between the buying patterns his agency encountered among smaller businesses and enterprise accounts. For SMB and mid-market programs with existing search demand, paid search offered a way to reach people actively researching a solution and establish acquisition benchmarks.

Enterprise programs often needed more education and time to engage a buying group, so his team leaned more heavily on paid social. He presented these as starting approaches, not a universal channel split for every business.

The channel decision also depended on what the buyer would encounter after the click. Saunders connected positioning, the offer, and creative: a demo request, an educational resource, and a product video served different needs. He described testing creative and landing-page content against the audience’s stage rather than expecting one asset to do every job.

The presenters emphasized defining a test’s business purpose before pitching a new platform. Saunders outlined three requirements: identify the problem, agree on the measurement and reporting cadence, and set a timeframe with a decision date.

For a lean budget, he recommended narrowing the audience or geography instead of spreading spend across a national market. A smaller test could investigate a specific segment, provided leadership understood what it could reveal and how long it needed to run.

He also stressed connecting advertising data with CRM outcomes. Form submissions could provide an early signal, but the team needed visibility into whether those leads became opportunities and customers. That distinction helped turn a request for more traffic into a business case for further investment.

Bruno’s connected TV example showed why the session’s testing walkthrough went beyond a campaign dashboard. CallRail initially saw encouraging website visits and trial activity from its CTV pilot through LinkedIn. Bruno cautioned that an ad exposure followed by a conversion did not establish that the ad caused it.

To investigate further, the team ran a 60-day holdout test with an audience eligible for CTV exposure and a control group that was not. Both groups entered the same downstream campaigns. Bruno described using the comparison to support a broader rollout, then monitoring acquisition efficiency as spend increased.

The useful lesson was the progression: early signals justified a more rigorous experiment, and that experiment informed the next investment decision. The pilot was a case study, not a guarantee that another advertiser would see the same result.

Bruno separated three ways of examining marketing’s contribution:

These views answered different questions. A rise in branded search could strengthen the case for further investigation; it was not interchangeable with a directly attributed conversion or proof of incremental revenue.

In their discussion of emerging LLM advertising, Saunders described limited reporting and the difficulty of evaluating indirect effects. The presenters also discussed self-reported attribution as another source of context, rather than treating any one measurement as the whole story.

During Q&A, an attendee asked whether Saunders’ recommendation to start enterprise programs with paid social meant LinkedIn. He said LinkedIn was typically the starting point, while paid search still had a role.

Bruno added a distinction between finding new prospects and re-engaging people who had already visited the site. The likely location of the buyer guided prospecting; retargeting could reach that same person elsewhere. Saunders described YouTube retargeting as one way to begin testing the channel before expanding into prospecting.

Google says ad tags in server-side Tag Manager will accept full IP addresses while Analytics tags stay redacted. Here's what changes and how to redact.

Server-side Google Tag Manager will let tags for Google’s ad products accept full IP addresses starting Jan. 11, 2027, according to a Google notice to advertisers.

The change covers tags that send data to Google Ads, Display & Video 360, Search Ads 360 and Campaign Manager 360 from a server container. Google Analytics tags will keep redacting IP addresses, the notice says.

Google Ads specialist Adriaan Dekker shared the notice on LinkedIn on Nov. 2. It carries no issue date, and Google’s Tag Manager release notes don’t mention the change as of Nov. 3.

Advertisers with Google ad tags in a server container have until Jan. 11 to decide whether those tags should get full or partially redacted IP addresses.

The notice, titled “Updates to network signal processing in server-side tagging,” explains that server containers “will transition from container-wide IP address redaction to individual tag-level processing.” It then outlines four effects:

Tags sending data to Google Ads, Display & Video 360, Search Ads 360 and Campaign Manager 360 will now accept the full IP address.

Google Analytics tags will continue to apply IP redaction.

Third-party tags will maintain independent control over the signals that they accept.

Transformations can redact these signals before any tag accesses the data.

The notice addresses server containers only. It says nothing about the Google tag or web containers running in the browser.

Google’s release notes show server-side Tag Manager could redact or anonymize IPs through Analytics server tags as of March 2021. Transformations, which edit or exclude event data before tags read it, followed in June 2023.

The notice doesn’t explain how container-wide redaction is currently set up. Google’s server-side setup page for the Google Ads conversion tag says the tag sends “all the available conversion data to Google” unless transformations change it, and, as of Nov. 3, doesn’t mention IP addresses.

The notice directs users to “our Help Centre article for detailed opt-out instructions” and does not reveal where the link is pointing to based upon the screenshot provided. A Tag Manager Help Center page, IP address redaction for server-side tagging, shows an example of how to use transformations.

The page outlines the main steps to set up this functionality using transformations:

This will affect the tags you choose (such as Google Ads or Floodlight). After completing these steps the page also states to check the results in Preview prior to deploying the changes to production. Additionally, the page explains that Analytics server tags “already apply partial IP redaction by default.”

Google’s API reference says the function zeroes the last octet of an IPv4 address and the last 80 bits of an IPv6 address. The Help page calls the result a “partially redacted IP.”

Google added the function to its API reference after Oct. 12. The Internet Archive’s Oct. 12 capture of the page doesn’t list it. The live page does, and shows an Oct. 30 update date.

Some third-party tags may need a Transformation of their own. The Help page notes that these tags can read IP addresses from custom headers or event parameters rather than from ip_override, so you’ll need to set the Transformation to target the field each tag uses.

The announcement does not provide information about how changes will interact with consent mode as well as the non-consenting requests that were stated in the Release Notes (Floodlight tags in server containers are said to have begun sending in July 2025) nor was there any mention of where or how long full IP addresses would be stored.

The announced server-side change is distinct from Google’s planned Analytics data control updates; these will encrypt IP addresses collected by the Google tag and SDK and pass them to linked Google Ads accounts, on dates Google plans to share later this year.

You can use server-side tagging to decide how much information goes with each tag as it leaves your servers, and Google’s notice determines whether its ad tags will accept full IP addresses in this configuration.

Prior to Jan. 11, review all Google Ads, Floodlight and third-party tags inside your server containers and identify which IP field each tag is reading. The method outlined by Google in the help section on how to build a Transformation using preview testing is currently the documented solution for keeping an ad tag’s IP partially masked. Your consent process should include any IP data used by these tags.

Tag-level IP processing for Google server containers is scheduled to begin January 11, 2027. There are no references to IP addresses in either of Google’s server-side pages on Transformations or consent mode as of Nov. 3.

The Tag Manager release notes may provide an official announcement when tag-level IP handling for server containers is available and the developer pages may have the detailed information. The Redaction help page should be reviewed prior to creating your Transformation because that is how you do this now.

AI Mode, AI Overviews, and traditional Search are becoming one product. What Google’s Q3 earnings call revealed about the agentic era.

Even though Wall Street is panicking over Google’s earnings call, it seems obvious to me what is happening. They are not going to slow down when it comes to AI. Throughout the call, they spoke of agents and how we are in the early days of how they are changing Search. They told us that AI Mode, AI overviews, and traditional Search are becoming one unified product.

They also said to expect rapid improvement because of Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI). Things are about to get very interesting.

I think new opportunities are arising, but also much of the way we have traditionally been able to make money from Search is disappearing.

If you prefer video, I share my thoughts on the call.

The main thing I took away from this earnings call is the emphasis on the shift to agentic search. I think this is still unfolding and no one fully knows what this new era of the web will look like. Google gave us a few hints in this call.

I find it fascinating how Google’s stock plummeted after this call. Alphabet’s revenues were up 25% YOY and Cloud revenue was up 103%. The general concern seems to be that Google is pushing AI Mode more, and so far there are fewer opportunities for ads shown in AI Mode. Therefore, revenue from Search is lower than expected. Still, Search advertising is up 12% YOY. (Wall Street was expecting 15%.)

I have no concerns over Google’s ability to continue to thrive. They mentioned in the call that their first priority is to make AI Mode a quality product and then it will focus more on monetizing it. Last week, Google announced that ads in AI Mode were expanding to more countries including Australia, Canada and more.

“Our approach is deliberate – prioritizing the user experience and engagement first, then scaling the formats.”

Mark my word, Google will make plenty of money from ads in the years to come. I think the new connected apps (see more on this below) could eventually be offered as ads.

They also spoke extensively about how there is incredible demand for Google’s computing power. It talked about TPUs not as chip sales, but as systems. “TPU Systems” were mentioned 35 times in the call. Thomas Kurian said:

“A TPU System is not just a chip, but it’s a specialized system that combines multiple things, including hardware, computer, storage, networking and so we are selling much more than just a chip. Software, training, inference.”

I mention this because Google will likely see incredible growth as more and more customers purchase these TPU systems.

What’s most interesting to me is how Google’s verbiage has shifted when it comes to talking about AI Mode and its relationship to Search.

The idea of traditional Search and AI Search merging into one product was mentioned several times:

“We are building one seamless experience across AI Overviews, AI Mode, and Traditional Search.”

“We think of Search holistically, a unified product spanning traditional results and AI powered Search.

I know it feels like Google is behind when it comes to having an agentic product. X has Grokbot. OpenAI has Dots, and Meta’s Muse is taking off. It seems clear to me that the vision of AI being our personal assistant has been in Google’s mind for some time. I think they’re taking their time to fully unpack it all because they need to get it right. Google’s end game here is not just an agent that will help us get things done online, but much bigger!

In May of 2025, Demis Hassabis wrote about Google’s dream of building what they called a “Universal AI Assistant.” Much of this piece discussed Google’s Genie world models acting as training environments for robots and how Project Astra which is now in Gemini Live, will allow us to have insight on the world around us. Google’s mission to organize the world’s information and make it universally accessible and useful.

I see the pieces coming together. It starts with online agents and will eventually expand into every aspect of our lives especially as the technology develops for intelligent eyewear and in-home robots.

“We are in the early stages of agentic experiences across our surfaces, and excited about the commercial opportunities ahead.”

He went on to speak about how they started by building agentic experiences into Gemini Enterprise first and, “as a next step [they’re] bringing these features to Search.”

“It’s clear that the agentic capabilities we all envision are going to be real.”

“I’m excited about agents, and I would view it as a new frontier, which brings in a new set of use cases to Search.”

Those new use cases likely start with Connected Apps.

By the way, if you want to be ahead of the curve in seeing how businesses are adapting to agentic search, I send out an email every week with all of the latest news on Search & AI:

On the day of the call, Google announced the Connected Apps Platform. There are already a handful of apps that can be used via MCP by Gemini either in the app or from within Search. Here is an example they gave where a user calls @Peloton to bring the Peloton app experience into their agentic flow within Gemini.

You can apply to the Connected Apps Platform here.

It was six months ago that Sundar Pichai said in an interview that “Search will be an agent manager.” I think this will be a new era where we shift from Search being a place to find websites that have information to a place where you use tools to help you (or your agents) get things done.

“The Gemini app is now at one billion users and is the fastest growing product in Google’s History.”

A billion users is the same number reported by ChatGPT in June of 2026.

I find this fascinating because my own use of the Gemini app has declined significantly. I use Gemini in Antigravity for almost everything.

We all know that Google’s models have not been as advanced as those from OpenAI and Anthropic.

Last week, Google announced a new frontier model, just two weeks after Gemini 4 Argon. Gemini 4 Carbon is currently undergoing voluntary testing as per the U.S. Government’s recommendations and will soon be released. Artificial Analysis currently has Carbon listed as the most intelligent model to date.

On the call, Sundar Pichai said that more models are coming soon, including “more efficient versions to help developers optimize for speed and cost.”

He said they started seeing a step change with Gemini 3.8 Flash when it came to coding internally at Google. And then Gemini 4 Argon was a “huge point of inflection.” He said:

“It is one of the most meaningful internal productivity levers [they] have seen on software engineering, directly tracking high-quality code that’s getting checked in, and the rate at which it’s getting checked in.”

“Carbon is a meaningful step up from Argon.”

Right now I use Gemini 4 Argon across three or four simultaneous Antigravity conversations most of the day long. On the Ultra plan, I have barely touched my quota. I thought 3.8 Flash was amazing. It helped me start to automate many of the SEO reports I run. When I switched to Gemini 4 Argon a mind blowing thing happened. Gemini 4 Argon + my internal OKF powered knowledge brain and my algo update MCP started producing far better consulting reports than I could alone. I truly believe we are not far from the day where AI will be better at all knowledge work than even the best humans in their field.

Last week, Google announced Genie 4, its latest world model. While it’s cool to see how it can generate interesting scenes and games, the most exciting thing about this model is that it will be used to create training simulations for AI agents and also for robots.

“Beyond our Gemini 4 series, yesterday we announced Genie 4, our most advanced world model yet that simulates safe, realistic, interactive worlds with native audio in real time. This is an important building block for training robots and agents.”

“I would expect the next twelve months to see continued acceleration because of RSI.”

Buckle up. RSI is “Recursive Self Improvement.” AI is being used more and more to help improve AI. We will see it improve rapidly.

Here’s the call if you’d like to listen to it.

#7426. Google’s Search Volume Is About 5x ChatGPT’s, OpenAI Says via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Webinar: 9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

ChatGPT's search-like queries equal about a fifth of Google's volume, its maker says, counting each question that sends it to the web. Traffic data differs.

ChatGPT receives roughly one-fifth as many search-like queries as does Google, according to ChatGPT consumer product lead Adam Fry.

The point he made about the volume of search-like queries was shared with Alex Kantrowitz in an open discussion during a Monday evening dinner in New York hosted by OpenAI. The transcript was later posted by Big Technology on Tuesday.

OpenAI counts a search each time a question sends ChatGPT to the web, Fry said. The visits ChatGPT sends to websites are a separate measure, and outside data on that traffic puts ChatGPT far behind Google.

Alex Kantrowitz of Big Technology asked Fry whether a conversation that includes a search counts as one, or whether each question requiring a web search counts separately. Fry replied:

“Every time you ask a question and go search the web, that’s a search.”

He said people first came to ChatGPT mostly for writing and coding help, which they wouldn’t have searched for. Over the past year, he said, they’ve brought questions about people, places and things that need up-to-date information, plus finance and health questions, where ChatGPT does a web search. He described the category as anything users would have taken to a traditional search engine.

Fry, in the published interview, did not reveal which Google figure was referenced; for how long the comparison is based on; nor does he state which regions are covered. He has also been asked if one-fifth of Google’s size makes ChatGPT multiple times bigger than Bing. The report by Big Technology indicates that the number of weekly active users of ChatGPT grew by 20% (from 1 billion to 1.2 billion) over the last two months.

In February, Ahrefs had estimated the search volume of ChatGPT to be around 12 percent that of Google’s search volume using a definition of search that was different from that used by OpenAI. It began with 2.5 billion daily ChatGPT prompts in July 2025 (from a study by Harvard University and OpenAI) and determined that approximately 65 percent were the type of query users would have previously looked up on Google.

Using this data, it compared those numbers with the over 5 trillion searches per year Google announced in March 2025. The author said that 65% was higher than the share the researchers had classified as search. That method sorts prompts by the kind of request, while Fry’s figure counts web searches.

Ahrefs also tracks where traffic to websites comes from across sites that use its free Web Analytics tool. In October, across 118,671 sites, Google accounted for 24.74% of tracked traffic and ChatGPT for 0.36%, according to the tracker’s Nov. 3 update.

Alphabet’s third-quarter release, which I covered on Oct. 28, gives Google’s search query growth as a rate rather than a count. In the release, CEO Sundar Pichai said AI investments are driving overall search query growth and that Google’s “year-over-year query growth rate is the highest it’s been in the last five years.”

OpenAI’s data comparing search-like queries by users of ChatGPT versus those using Google indicates the approximate 1/5th ratio. Fry’s counting rule includes only the search requests made by ChatGPT users in order to send a question to the Web. Ahrefs’ referral tracker tracks the number of visitors that are directed to websites. In this data set, Google has an overwhelming amount of referrals compared to ChatGPT.

Neither Fry’s number nor Google’s year-over-year growth rate illustrates if ChatGPT searches are replacing searches on Google. If ChatGPT’s size is included in a channel plan, then when reporting search it should be accompanied by the definitions of query volume and referral traffic, which will provide two different metrics.

Ahrefs’ tracker reports referral shares month by month, giving you a regular outside perspective on the traffic ChatGPT sends. OpenAI’s roughly one-fifth ratio is difficult to compare with other estimates until the company clarifies which Google figure it used.
