#7423. Reddit’s Logged-In Future: Why Its Pull In Search And AI Answers Isn’t Fading via @sejournal, @brentcsutoras

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: 9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

Reddit conversations still shape purchase decisions through search and AI, giving brands reasons to stay engaged and watch how login tests affect access.

Reddit’s Q3 Earnings Call got a lot of attention in the last few days, specifically for an announcement to start moving towards a more logged-in experience. I understand the attention and worry some marketers have expressed, but having listened to the entire conversation, as well as the ModWorld AMA interview, I do not find myself concerned about the future of Reddit or its influence in search and LLMs.

I will get into that more in a second, but another really big point worth highlighting is how important Reddit has become to the user’s journey online.

Reddit reported an average of 515.2 million weekly active uniques in Q3. That isn’t a count of people shopping, but it gives some context for the size of the platform where these decisions are being discussed.

In my experience, Google often helps people narrow their options, and Reddit helps them validate the decision. Once someone has figured out which products might solve their problem, they want to know what happened when another person actually used them, what went wrong, and whether the recommendation still makes sense for their situation.

In Reddit’s May 2026 survey, half of the U.S. respondents said they verify AI recommendations on Reddit.*

In its Q3 shareholder letter and earnings call, Reddit said it plans to begin testing a logged-in experience in select markets outside the U.S. during Q4. Steve Huffman was clear that Reddit is going to make this change, but the tests will help figure out where and when someone needs to log in.

He also said Reddit wants shared links to keep working and described leaving some access available for people coming from search, opening a shared post, or trying Reddit for the first time. My reading is that someone could still get to the conversation they came for, with the login requirement appearing as they try to go further into Reddit. Reddit still needs to figure out where that login prompt belongs.

That’s a familiar approach for a social platform, and Huffman pointed to peers that have already made this transition. Reddit wants more people using a personalized experience, better signals for advertising, and more control over access to its data. I can see why Reddit would want those things, even if someone dropping in to read a conversation would rather skip the account.

I would still watch what happens in the tests because asking people to log in can affect whether they stay, come back, or join the conversation. Keeping a linked post accessible also doesn’t guarantee that Google’s rankings stay the same or that every LLM can continue accessing Reddit in the same way. But I didn’t hear a reason to jump straight to the conclusion that Reddit is shutting off discovery through search and AI.

Huffman also said data licensing discussions are continuing, including access for training and use within products. There wasn’t a new deal announced, and he left open the possibility of declining a deal. Those conversations are worth following alongside the login tests, without assuming that one tells us how the other will turn out.

See also: Reddit Wants To Be The Destination, Not Just The Source Behind Search & AI

Reddit was already receiving less search traffic before these login tests. Huffman said the decline accelerated during Q3 and continued into October. He pointed to Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode as major factors, with lower rankings for machine-translated content as another possible explanation.

Pew’s study of U.S. browsing in March 2025 found that people clicked a traditional result on 8% of visits with an AI summary, compared with 15% without one. A link within the summary received a click on 1% of visits with a summary. That isn’t a measurement of Reddit’s current traffic, but it gives us some context for the click-through concerns.

Fewer clicks don’t mean those Reddit threads aren’t being used. I see Reddit conversations referenced in AI Overviews all the time, helping shape the answers people get. Someone can learn from that conversation and use it to make a decision without opening the thread.

People can still click through from an AI Overview, and those visits still matter. From a search marketing standpoint, I also see value in Reddit threads showing up in the results, being referenced in an answer, and helping shape what people learn about a brand or product.

See also: Reddit Preserved The Part Of The Internet We Broke

These are the conversations where people get into whether a product will work for their situation, what went wrong when someone else used it, and which trade-offs they’re willing to accept. Someone explains their circumstances, another person challenges a recommendation, and the replies bring out a detail that changes the decision.

If people keep asking the same question about your product, there’s something they haven’t been able to figure out. If they keep recommending a competitor for a particular situation, there’s a reason worth understanding. Being present gives you an opportunity to learn from those conversations and help where your experience is relevant, while respecting how that community works.

Those same conversations can help shape what someone learns about your brand when they find them through search or see them referenced in an AI answer. I would want to understand what people are saying, where they’re getting stuck, and what someone from the company could explain that would help them make a decision.

It always makes me think back to something my co-founder at OGS Media, Bartosz Goralewicz, once said: “Reddit is the only website I know of that told search engines, ‘Pay us, or we’ll pull our content.'”

Reddit’s a continuously evolving platform, and its place online keeps adjusting and shifting, but those conversations continue to be valuable, both to the people making decisions and to the search and AI platforms using them.

*Survey source: Reddit/Attest, May 2026. The survey covered U.S. adults ages 18-65 who use social media, LLMs, and ecommerce monthly, with a full U.S. sample of 13,956 respondents.

#7422. Google’s News AI pilot expands to over 400 publications, including U.S. local news outlets

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

In December, Google launched its News AI pilot program, which licenses content from select publishers and uses it to test new AI features in Google News. On Thursday, the company announced that the program has added new partnerships, bringing the total number of publications in the pilot to more than 400 worldwide.

At launch, the program partnered with international publishers like The Guardian, El País, The Times of India, and The Washington Post. More publications are now coming on board, including CNN, The Financial Times, Axios, and Forbes.

RELATED ARTICLEDiscover isn’t the only place Google is experimenting with AI-generated snippetsAndrew DeckJanuary 26, 2026As part of the expansion, the program has also added local news publishers across the U.S., including The Post and Courier in Charleston, South Carolina; Oil City News in Casper, Wyoming; the Illinois- and Iowa-based newspaper chain Shaw Media; and the nonprofit newsroom The Texas Tribune.

“People’s information consumption habits are changing, and we want to make sure publishers of all sizes, local newsrooms included, can navigate these shifts,” Brianna Puccini Duff, a spokesperson for Google, said in a statement to Nieman Lab.

Google declined to comment on the exact terms of the deals. However, Duff clarified that the News AI pilot does not operate on a “pay-per-value” model, meaning publishers are not compensated based on how much their content contributes to an AI-generated output. (The pay-per-value model is part of a parallel program that pays publishers for content surfaced in AI Overviews, AI Mode, and Gemini, according to a recent report by Digiday.)

With the News AI pilot, publishers are instead paid to provide content that appears in experimental AI-powered features. That includes “story previews” — in-depth, AI-generated article summaries of recent stories that may show up on a publisher’s Google News page. Here’s a Washington Post example, with a disclaimer noting the copy is AI-generated and “may include mistakes.”

An AI-generated “story preview” on the Google News page for The Washington Post

Another test feature is “audio briefing,” a customizable, AI-generated podcast in the Google News app that stitches together daily headlines. Users can select the topics they’re most interested in hearing about, including “World,” “Gaming,” or “Sports” news. The feature includes citations that link to articles mentioned in the briefing.

The most important stories about journalism and the future of news, delivered to your inbox every afternoon.

The unrestricted funding helped small outlets plug holes and try new things, but publishers ran up against the limits of what two $50,000 grants could accomplish, especially when it came to hiring.

Need another reason to read that 47,212th article about paywall strategy? What if it earned you a point?

#7421. A new report argues newsrooms need to do more experiments — like, the kind with randomization and results

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Mississippi Today had a question. Did the stories around its Pulitzer Prize-winning investigative reporting affect the way those investigations were received?

It’s the kind of question local newsrooms can’t easily test on their own. But researchers from Local NExT Lab at Syracuse University could.

In a national survey, 1,768 adults were shown the same investigation surrounded by a different mix of stories. In one, the investigation was shown alongside positive community stories. (Think: “How a local fossil park changed science history.”) In another, the investigation was featured alongside other investigative stories.

The investigation was rated more accurate, important, and relevant when it was surrounded by community-focused stories, not other investigative stories. (Audience reaction to a third story mix, where the investigation was surrounded by stories about legislation, was not consistent.)

The result was described in the first report from the Local NExT Lab. Joshua Darr, director of the lab and associate professor at Syracuse University, believes that although dashboards and engagement analytics are “very important tools” for newsrooms, they aren’t enough.

“Engagement data can’t tell you what caused audiences to engage, settle a hunch, or isolate your contribution,” the report reads. “Randomization can.”

“The key word there is ’caused,'” Darr added in an email. “Without randomization, you can tell when engagement is up or down or if a particular story is doing well, but it’s hard to know exactly why that is happening.”

RELATED ARTICLESearching for gold: Making sense of academic research about journalismAngie Drobnic HolanApril 27, 2023At Nieman Lab, we often hear from both sides of academic-practitioner partnerships. Researchers wonder why newsrooms don’t pay attention to their findings or fail to respond to their overtures about experiments. Publishers, editors, and journalists, meanwhile, tell me they don’t have time to read dense and jargon-filled academic papers. They can be annoyed by requests to spend time or resources they don’t have. And it’s not always fun to be someone else’s test subject.

When partnering with Local NExT Lab, Darr emphasized, the local newsrooms don’t have to commit money or manpower. They agree to two or three conversations. The researchers listen and then design, field, and analyze the experiments. In return, the newsrooms get their ideas tested and causal evidence.

In another experiment, the Local NExt Lab found that Instagram Reels including reporters’ faces drove the most interest and engagement, but when it came to clicking “follow,” profiles that looked like traditional news brands won out. Respondents chose to follow newsrooms (in this case New Orleans Public Radio) more often than reporter-named accounts.

The first batch of tests was funded by the W.K. Kellogg Foundation. Additional support from the American Journalism Project will allow for further tests on a larger cohort next year. The full report is here.

#7419. Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Starting October 30, business accounts will consent to Meta scraping their websites if they continue using Facebook, Instagram, or WhatsApp.

Meta can use web scrapers to crawl and collect content from websites “associated with” business accounts on its platforms, according to its new commercial terms of use.

The update, set to go into effect on October 30, will include news publishers with business accounts. These accounts allow companies or public figures to manage Facebook pages, Messenger accounts, Instagram profiles, or WhatsApp channels from one place. While journalism isn’t the only industry that will be affected by this update, virtually every news organization has at least one Meta business account, including Nieman Lab.

The new terms broadly cover business accounts that manage pages and groups, run advertisements, push marketing messages, and use the platform’s business account dashboard. As written, the new terms could be used to argue that Meta can scrape content from news sites and use that content to train the company’s AI products, according to three legal experts who reviewed the terms at Nieman Lab’s request.

RELATED ARTICLE“An astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions”: Court records show what Microsoft and OpenAI actually thought about AI trainingSarah ScireSeptember 18, 2026“This is a remarkable provision to bury in [the] terms of service, given that this would give Meta access to material that would likely cost many millions of dollars in a licensing market,” said Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “It’s not clear whether a court would enforce this, but publishers should assume that it would be enforceable.”

In early October, Meta alerted users to the update in a blog post and on the Meta Business Suite. The updated terms explicitly state that Meta can use the content it collects from associated websites to “train” Meta products. Elsewhere in its terms of service, the company defines “AI at Meta” as one of those products.

Here’s the new language about scraping in full:

You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.

“For news publishers, this clearly represents permission to Meta to train AI on any content from their sites and possibly to deploy some of that content, even in competition with the publishers themselves,” said James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School. “On the broadest possible interpretation, this would be used to develop a comprehensive archive of all content that Meta would then serve as it wanted to directly or through AI.”

Currently, there is no option for business accounts to opt out of these new terms ahead of October 30. The update reads, “If you do not agree to the updated terms, please stop all access or use of our Products for business or commercial purposes.”

Meta declined to answer a list of questions about these updated terms. A public affairs spokesperson at the company said in an email that language around crawling was previously scattered across different terms of use, including terms about using generative AI in ads, and this update consolidates them in one place. He also said that the new terms will not change how Meta crawls publishers in the future, and that “content owners can still manage how their content is accessed by using robots.txt.”

On its developer page, Meta currently has instructions for how to block its crawlers using robots.txt, a file that tells bots which parts of a website they can and cannot access.

However, legal experts said the new language creates an opening for Meta to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions. The update also states that Meta can create “test credentials” in order to scrape websites associated with business accounts. Grimmelmann said this would technically allow Meta to “sign up as a fake user” to bypass registration walls on a publisher’s site to access content. Meta declined to answer Nieman Lab’s questions about whether the “test credentials” would bypass paywalls or other paid content.

RELATED ARTICLEFederal appeals court upholds Thomson Reuters’ landmark AI copyright winAndrew DeckSeptember 30, 2026Any attempt to train Meta’s AI products with content collected under these new terms would still hinge on unsettled legal questions about AI training and fair use, legal experts said. Several lawsuits between publishers and AI developers are currently winding their way through federal courts. That includes a class-action suit filed in May by five large book publishers, alleging Meta pirated millions of books in order to train its Llama large language models (LLMs).

Meta’s decision to tether access to its business products to broad scraping permissions echoes a concept in antitrust law called “tying,” according to Benjamin Sobel, a law professor at the University of Wisconsin. “If you want to use the Meta products that require acceptance of the commercial terms, you have to also acquiesce to the scraping and crawling permissions exacted in those terms.”

Sobel compared the move to Google’s recent policies around its AI search products. In order to appear in Google’s traditional search results, publishers previously had to consent to their content appearing in AI Overviews and AI Mode. As of August 2026, all websites now have the option to opt out.

Meta’s new commercial terms come on the heels of the company’s rollout of its paid subscription service, Meta One. The cash-for-links program restricts the number of external links that some accounts on Facebook and Instagram can post without subscribing. Put another way, Meta has begun charging users to post links to the same content that it will be permitted to crawl for free. Earlier this month, Press Gazette reported that some news publishers are currently exempt from the link limit. Meta declined to answer Nieman Lab’s question about the service.

RELATED ARTICLEMeet the journalists training AI models for Meta and OpenAIAndrew DeckFebruary 20, 2025Nieman Lab first learned about Meta’s new commercial terms through a reader tip. Stephen Beale, the founder and editor of The Steampunk Explorer, got in touch when he saw a notice of the upcoming change in his Meta Business Suite dashboard.

“Traditionally, you have this idea that Meta might be using content [posted] on Facebook or Instagram for training,” Beale told Nieman Lab. “But this was different because they’re saying that [since you are] a business user of Facebook, they have the right to go out and grab information from basically wherever you have a presence.”

Beale has long depended on Facebook as a way to connect with his audience and refer traffic to his site. Fans of steampunk — a retrofuturistic subgenre of science fiction — skew older, he said, and the community is “totally entrenched on Facebook.” For many, their only interactions with the community happen on Facebook or at in-person events that they learned about on Facebook.

Beale said he’s seriously considering shutting down his accounts before October 30.

“I know my site has been scraped to death,” he said. “But it just seems like such an arrogant, in-your-face move on [Meta’s] part… It just makes me angry and I don’t want them to get away with it.”

Are you considering changing how you use Meta-owned platforms? Let us know at [email protected].

Correction: This story has been updated to reflect Google’s current AI search policies.

#7418. Your CMS Is Still Failing SEO Basics – 11 Fixes To Demand via @sejournal, @sallymills

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: 9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

Cut recurring developer tickets with CMS SEO essentials like canonical tags and indexing controls, plus automation, redirect safeguards, and real examples.

Content management systems (CMS) often try to force SEOs into a box of “this is how a website should work.” The problem is that SEO has never been a black-and-white thing and so often depends upon the individual website, industry, and brand as to how we may want to structure indexing, content, and infrastructure.

Over my years as an in-house SEO, consultant, and web developer, I’ve worked with a wide range of CMS. Even though we continue to see improvements across platforms, many still fail to meet the base-level requirements and flexibility we as SEOs need day-to-day. This results in us as an industry being on repeat, submitting the same ticket for a fix again and again.

What do I consider to be the actual bare minimum a CMS should offer for SEOs and content creators? Every week I continue to find out about often well-known platforms missing what I would consider a baseline standard.

On three different systems this year, I’ve watched teams need a developer to implement canonical tags – Google, Microsoft, and Yahoo announced the tag together back in 2009! You’d think we’d have this sorted by now.

On Webflow, I’ve had to hardcode HTML tables into the page because the editor doesn’t have built-in HTML table support. I’ve found having semantically correct HTML incredibly important to help bots understand the content.

And on WordPress, you have no way to edit your robots.txt out-of-the-box, exclude pages from the sitemap, or noindex individual pages without the help of a developer or accessing your source files. This often forces users to install bloated SEO plugins to manage what I would consider the basics of SEO.

In my opinion, every CMS that considers SEO, and wants to be crawlable and accessible by bots, should have the following:

If your content is a list, show it in an unordered or ordered list.

If your content is in the sidebar, put it in an aside HTML element.

I’ve recently seen this issue with Shopify preventing you from removing pages from sitemaps when you are using an additional market as sitemaps “are generated automatically and include all market-specific URLs.”

I’ve worked across numerous platforms over my time with many having a constant stream of content, development, and marketing changes going live. Often teams find themselves raising the same ticket again and again. Over the years, there have been a few CMS improvements that development teams and I have implemented to help improve speed to market.

See also: Ask An SEO: How Do You Prioritize Technical SEO Fixes With Limited Dev Support?

Having a table of contents at the start of your content is hugely beneficial to the user and can earn you sitelinks in Google’s search results. Often, systems can make this quite a manual job to create, forcing the content creator to manually create each link and ID tag for the headings of the page.

A good CMS should automate this task completely by grabbing the H2s of the page and pulling them into the component. To go above and beyond, they should also allow you to exclude specific headings and choose whether to include H3s and H4s.

I’ve had to get this built by a developer in enterprise CMSs. Even WordPress needs a plugin like Rank Math to do it, which tells you how far down the list it sits for most platforms.

SEOs can often become maintenance people, cleaning up broken links, redirecting pages that are gone, then, of course, cleaning up internal links that are now redirecting. There are a few different levels of automation that CMSs could offer to reduce the manual workload of SEOs.

I’ve worked on large editorial websites where there simply isn’t the resource to go through and replace each link that redirects.

The biggest run I’ve done was after a migration of a site with tens of thousands of URLs from an old .NET platform to a new CMS. Every internal link on the site still pointed at the old URL and hopped through a redirect to get to the new one. We wrote a Python script against the CMS API that followed each link to its final destination and rewrote it, so nobody had to fix links by hand.

Having this script run regularly ensures bots spend less time on old URLs, users get to their destinations quicker, and the business spends less time on manual cleanup tasks.

A CMS should also be flagging when a page’s URL has been changed and automatically adding a 301 redirect from the old URL to the new. This change would reduce delayed clean-up from SEOs and would result in a better user experience.

If they wanted to go above and beyond, a clean-up script should be scheduled to automatically update any internal links that still point to the old URL. Extra points if the system could suggest a relevant URL to redirect to.

We often have to rely on technical SEO tools to report on 404 errors. I think in today’s world of monitoring, CMSs should offer offer a report of broken links and allow SEOs to bulk upload the correct links or decide to remove the link. So often, we find ourselves having to edit 404 links one by one – and often the same link.

It’s still incredibly rare that we have systems that offer the functionality to set a URL or a folder of URLs to a 410 status code. To this day, I’ve only used a 410 a few times on a live site. With most CMSs not providing this functionality, SEOs tend to land on redirecting or leaving as a 404.

Most platforms these days have some form of redirect manager; however, so often they are missing important customization and safeguards.

Guardrails matter more than any other item on this list. I once took an entire website down with a single stray pipe character in a regex redirect rule. One | in the wrong place matched every URL on the site and sent all of them to the same page. A redirect manager that tested the rule against a sample of URLs before saving would have caught it in seconds.

To this day, I haven’t found a CMS that does a great job of handling different image files. Often they’ll have a range of issues that negatively impact SEO.

One of my biggest gripes is the messy and multiple different versions of an image URL. One enterprise system I’ve worked with would add an ID to every image file, and applying different optimizations like sizing or cropping within the platform would result in numerous different URLs. And you could still reference the image directly without the ID. For websites where image search is vital, this could cause major duplication issues.

Previously, it was an absolute requirement for me to have a CMS that allowed for either bulk importing content changes through CSV or API alongside a Python script. With the way AI is changing our work processes, having the ability to connect your AI agent through CLI or MCP is incredibly helpful.

As of this year, I’m finding myself making fewer changes directly in a CMS and instead connecting to MCPs or CLI. If you are running your own WordPress environment, I would recommend testing out the Claude Code and CLI connection. On some of my websites, I can now update content and development work directly from Claude.

As always with anything AI and connecting to public websites, make sure you have testing processes and guardrails set up to ensure that you don’t break anything important.

In big businesses, we often see repeatable small tickets take up developers’ time that simply require them to upload a new marketing script to the HTML head or the top of the body. One of the best time-saving opportunities is to provide a CMS settings section that allows you to add scripts manually.

In the past, this has given me the flexibility to quickly trial new schemas, tracking tools, and metadata.

However, this does require trust between the development and marketing teams, as it is a way to break something. So always include code validation and a release process to protect your website.

Every CMS is going to be different, so the best thing you can do is work with what you have. People often ask me for a CMS recommendation, and in very SEO style I say, “It depends.” And often, we aren’t the person who gets to make that decision.

I encourage everyone to problem-solve and try to automate where possible. Analyze where you or the team are spending most of your time and which tickets keep coming up time and time again. Work closely with developers to build out solutions that can grow as the business grows and give you the flexibility to implement yourself.

#7415. Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Allowing scraped content to be used for all “advertising and business products” is a substantial expansion of Meta’s permissions.

RELATED ARTICLEMeta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts sayAndrew DeckOctober 15, 2026Meta has removed the word “train” from its upcoming terms of service for business accounts. The company revised its terms after Nieman Lab’s story on Thursday exposed that the new terms would permit broad scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts, and possibly allow Meta to use that scraped content to train its AI models.

In its revision, published Friday afternoon, Meta removed the word “train” from a list of allowed use cases and limited those uses to “advertising and business products,” rather than all Meta products. But the revised terms will still allow for broad scraping of websites, potentially superseding robots.txt files, according to legal experts.

On Saturday, a Meta spokesperson said the company revised the terms because “it wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.”

Meta has not included any specific language about respecting robots.txt preferences in its revised terms of service. The new terms are slated to go into effect on October 30. There is no option for business accounts to opt out of the new terms before then.

“I think publishers should remain concerned,” said Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “The revised version of the new terms still allows Meta to use that scraped content to develop any ‘business product.’ That doesn’t seem to be a defined term, and presumably Meta is developing AI business products. I think ‘develop’ is broad enough to include ‘train.'”

Meta currently lists examples of its business products as “ads, Meta Business Tools and Meta Business Suite.”

Virtually every news organization has at least one Meta business account. The accounts let companies manage Facebook pages, Threads accounts, Instagram profiles, and WhatsApp channels from one place.

As of publication time, the section reads (with changes in bold):

You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs in order to provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products (including business, commercial and related products to help you create and deliver ads and other commercial content, provide users information about your products and services, and connect you with users who may be interested in your products and services) and maintain the integrity and security of Meta Company Products. Here’s the original text: You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms. “We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves,” a spokesperson said in a statement, claiming publishers can still update their scraping preferences using robots.txt files. “This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.” Meta’s current terms permit it to scrape websites associated with business accounts, but only in a very specific scenario. That language is found in its terms of service for when accounts use Meta’s generative AI features to run advertisements. The scraped content can only be used to “optimize your ads.” Meta's controversial termsOctober 15Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts sayOctober 17 ★Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changesOctober 21U.K. politicians and German publishers call on regulators to pause Meta’s new terms before October 30 deadlineOctober 22Publishers pressure Meta to nix new terms that would let the company scrape their websitesOctober 26Meta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. “We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves,” a spokesperson said in a statement, claiming publishers can still update their scraping preferences using robots.txt files. “This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”

Meta’s current terms permit it to scrape websites associated with business accounts, but only in a very specific scenario. That language is found in its terms of service for when accounts use Meta’s generative AI features to run advertisements. The scraped content can only be used to “optimize your ads.”

A Meta spokesperson said the company is incorporating its “Ad Creative Generative AI Terms” into its general commercial terms to make them easier to understand.

Three legal experts Nieman Lab consulted were skeptical about the revised terms of service and Meta’s most recent statements.

“[The update] doesn’t address my concerns,” said James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School. “While it adds more language about the permitted uses, [the] ‘develop…advertising and business products’ [language] is still broad enough to drive a truck through. This does nothing to restrict the ‘associated with your products or services’ [language] that would let Meta scrape entire sites.”

University of Wisconsin law professor Benjamin Sobel explained that robots.txt indicates a website’s preferences, but compliance with those is completely voluntary. He likened it to a homeowner putting up a sign saying, “Don’t look at my house.” Putting up that sign doesn’t give the homeowner an enforceable legal right to stop people from looking at the house.

“You can still express the preference, and unless it’s a legally enforceable preference, it can still be ignored all the same,” he said.

“This shameless landgrab attempt from Meta to scrape anything and everything from news publishers and business websites to train their AI products is the worst kind of arrogant tech platform bullying,” said chief executive Theo Bamber. “We urgently need Ministers and regulators to stand up for British creators and the business community by calling out this outrageous behaviour and preventing Meta from setting this dreadful precedent.”

The News/Media Alliance — the largest news publishing trade association in the United States — denounced the terms, with president and CEO Danielle Coffey calling the update “outrageous and probably illegal.”

#7414. “Convenings” for CEOs will help Semafor reach a second profitable year

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Semafor expects to have its second profitable year, thanks to a growing events, er, convening business, cofounders Justin Smith and Ben Smith announced.

The news company, which launched four years ago, had its first profitable year last year on $40 million in revenue. In a note published Sunday, Smith and Smith said they expect to close the year “substantially bigger” in “revenue and profitability and reach.”

RELATED ARTICLEThe media startup Semafor launches with a “more honest” article format and lots of global ambitionSarah ScireOctober 18, 2022About half of the company’s revenue comes from live events, which Semafor refers to as “convenings.” A two-day convening in November, for example, will cover “Silicon Valley & The World.” The co-chairs include names like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella.

In their note, the cofounders wrote that “Semafor is starting to emerge clearly as the thing that we hoped it would become.”

RELATED ARTICLESemafor aims to be the source for “intelligent news consumers” who are “unhappy” and “screaming from the rooftops”Sarah ScireSeptember 7, 2022“We launched with the insight that a leadership audience — CEOs and political leaders alike — was, paradoxically, the most desperate for efficient, fair, and sophisticated news,” they continued.

It’s a stretch to say CEOs and political leaders are “desperate” for news. Existing news consumers tend to be older, wealthier, more white collar, and more politically engaged than those who don’t consume news. The genuinely underserved news audiences are elsewhere. Journalism for “decision makers” is one of the most crowded markets in news. Outlets like Bloomberg, Politico Pro, Financial Times, Punchbowl News, Axios Pro, and The Information operate in a similar space.

But readers aren’t the primary financial supporters of Semafor’s business. That’d be the corporate sponsors paying for access to its audience through ads and events. Although the annual update says the company has 1.2 million subscriptions, those remain free subscriptions for now.

By building a profitable and growing news business, Semafor has done something exceedingly rare. (It now has journalists on the ground in 11 countries and plans to launch in Asia in 2027.) Editor-in-chief Ben Smith explained some of his thinking on an episode of Decoder this summer.

In my memory, we always thought at some point we’d do subscriptions, but in my experience you just cannot be ideological about revenue. It’s hard enough to build a business in news without getting all hung up on the values of the different revenue streams.

Advertising-based publishers will tell you that democracy can only survive in a world where there aren’t paywalls. Subscription publishers will tell you that advertising is corrupting. At some point you realize everyone’s just talking about their book and that sometimes they’re already in a tough business and they’re talking themselves out of incremental opportunities and really successful media companies.

It’s “impossible” for publishers to compete with Google and Meta in the scaled advertising business, Smith told Decoder. He described Semafor as “an anti-scale business.”

If you’re reaching people in a very focused way in various particular environments — in person, in email, in video — that’s a case you can really credibly make to advertisers. We’ve built a big advertising and related convening business that way, and that’s one answer. It’s not the only answer, but it is one.

#7412. Reach Is No Longer The KPI: 4 Signals From Jupiter Festival Miami That Reset 2027 Media Budgets via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: 9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

Build your 2027 paid media plan around attention, creator content, and streaming inventory, with tests that tie new metrics to incremental sales.

If you manage paid search, paid social, or programmatic budgets, the first Jupiter Festival Miami just handed you a 2027 planning problem. The executives who buy and sell premium video spent three days saying that reach is no longer the number that matters. And the money is already moving toward creators, attention-weighted media, and new streaming inventory to back that up.

That matters to PPC people more than it might seem. When the people setting brand budgets change the KPI, the performance team eventually inherits the new scorecard.

I’ve been looking for signals like this at industry conferences since I entered the field in 2002. The speakers at the good ones share strategic insights, critical data, and tactical advice that fly under the radar, because organizers know conventional wisdom won’t fill seats or bring attendees back next year. So, they book people who work at the leading edge of the leading edge.

Jupiter Festival ran from Oct. 6 to 9, 2026, at the Miami Beach Convention Center. Its organizers say more than 2,300 media, entertainment, and sports leaders attended. Art Basel’s parent, MCH Group, took a 20% stake in June. The IAB signed up as a founding partner, and YouTube was the founding sponsor.

I didn’t attend. But I reviewed the daily recaps the festival’s publicists sent me, then checked what the speakers said against published data. Four signals held up.

Jasmine Dawson, senior VP of digital at BBC Studios, on a Day 1 panel about building fandoms that brands can activate said, “Reach should not be the primary KPI.” A big reach number is great for the media owner, she added, but it says nothing about whether the audience will do anything next.

Her distinction was that “building an audience is not fandom and fandom is not audience.”

On Day 2, Marc Guldimann, CEO and co-founder of Adelaide, put a measurement frame around the same idea. “If you want to rate the quality of an opportunity, look at the probability of attention,” he said during a panel with YouTube’s U.S. managing director Brian Albert and Evan Shapiro of ESHAP. Brands, he added, are now telling the whole ecosystem that they care more about quality.

That isn’t a throwaway line from Guldimann. Adelaide’s AU metric scores media placements from 0 to 100 on their likelihood of capturing attention and driving outcomes. Its 2026 Outcomes Guide covers 60 campaigns. And on Oct. 14, a week after Miami, the company launched a partner designation program for survey and outcome partners whose data can be matched directly to AU.

Shapiro pushed the argument furthest. Three days before he unveiled the 2026 Creator Ecosphere Map on stage on Oct. 8, he previewed it in a Substack post headlined “The Era of Reach is Over. Welcome to The Affinity Era.” The map ranks creators by follower count and, alongside that, grades each one on an affinity score.

Three speakers from three corners of the business, the seller, the measurement vendor, and the analyst, landed in the same place. That’s what an emerging trend looks like before it shows up in a platform’s reporting interface.

Here’s my take. Paid search people will be tempted to shrug, because search has never been a reach business. But your YouTube, CTV, and Demand Gen line items probably still report on impressions, CPM, and view rate. Those are reach metrics. If the brand side starts asking for quality-weighted numbers in 2027, the performance team that already has them will own that conversation.

See also: How Do I Measure And Attribute When Clicks Only Tell Part Of The Story? – Ask A PPC

The Day 3 panel “Direct to Fan: How Creators Are Building the New Media Stack” included Amanda Tarpey, head of creator and creative at YouTube Ads. Her read on advertisers was that marketers are “waking up” to the trust, influence, and authenticity creators have. “They’re saying: I can’t afford to miss that,” she said. “There’s a lot of experimentation, but the infrastructure is not standardized.”

That second sentence is the one PPC teams should underline.

The IAB’s own numbers show why. Its 2025 Creator Economy Ad Spend & Strategy Report found that 48% of creator ad buyers now consider creators a “must buy,” ranking them just behind paid search and social media. The report put U.S. creator ad spend at $37.1 billion in 2025 and projected $43.9 billion for 2026, according to Digiday’s breakdown of the report.

The split is where paid media comes in. Digiday reports that $13.2 billion of the 2026 total is expected to go to paid amplification of creator content on social media, up 48% from $8.9 billion. Another $11.1 billion goes to amplifying that content beyond social, up 56% from $7.1 billion. In other words, a growing share of “creator marketing” is really ad buying with creator-made creative.

The creators on stage explained the pull. Joakim Noah, the former NBA player who hosts the YouTube series NOMAD, said what he loves about YouTube is controlling his content and “connecting with an audience that is completely different from what you’re used to.” Hudson Matter, a YouTuber and CEO of NextWave Media, called YouTube “one of the most powerful platforms in the world.”

One correction is needed, though. Matter also said, “almost half of the world is on YouTube.” Alphabet doesn’t publish a monthly user count, but DataReportal puts YouTube’s ad reach at about 2.77 billion people a month, roughly a third of the world’s population. That’s closer to half of internet users than half of the world. Use the smaller number in your deck.

My view is that Tarpey’s “not standardized” warning is the real opportunity here. When the infrastructure is messy, the team that can run creator content through the same testing, bidding, and conversion tracking discipline it applies to search ads becomes the team that gets the budget.

See also: Why Running YouTube Ads Like Search Will Burn Your Budget

Scott Young, co-founder and chief product officer of Transmit, made the most practical point of Day 1. “With streaming, you have the opportunity to aggregate valuable ad supply that would have otherwise gotten lost,” he said. He singled out women’s sports, which he said are growing on free ad-supported streaming.

Transmit is the plumbing behind that claim. Its software creates in-stream ad units, such as picture-in-picture placements during live games, without adding more traditional ad breaks. The company was selected for the Google Ad Manager Technology Partner Program, which connects that “in-moment” inventory to Google Ad Manager’s programmatic pipes for live and on-demand video.

For anyone buying through Google’s stack or a DSP, that’s the part to watch. New premium sports inventory that used to be sold only through direct deals is starting to show up as programmatic supply.

The women’s sports thread ran through all three days. On Day 2, WNBA legend Lisa Leslie talked about welcoming new fans while staying true to loyal ones. Colie Edison, the WNBA’s chief growth officer, said customers are “three times more likely to purchase from a brand that they support.” I couldn’t find the study behind that number, so treat it as a claim, not a benchmark. On Day 3, LA Sparks president Stacy Johns said it’s on the teams “to create the content and interesting moments for brands to show up authentically.”

There’s a budgeting catch for 2027, too. NBCUniversal Telemundo’s Claudia Chagui described turning Rockefeller Center into a FIFA World Cup fan village this summer. Big live events like that, plus a costly U.S. midterm cycle, inflated 2026. EMARKETER projects total U.S. media ad spending growth will slow from 15.6% in 2026 to 9.4% in 2027, and it warns that CTV budgets built around tournament and election inventory should expect to normalize.

Anish Melwani, former chairman and CEO of LVMH North America and co-founder of 22 Montaigne Entertainment, described a decade-long tug of war that every performance marketer will recognize. Luxury marketing evolved toward “more lower funnel performance,” he said, “but great luxury brands understand how much you have to keep doing at the top in order for that to make a difference.”

He also drew a line between formats. Luxury will keep looking for “pockets of premium,” he said, while other brands look at two-minute microdramas, and the two occupy different places in consumers’ minds.

Shapiro predicted the same format shift from the other direction. “Like cable in the ’80s, you will see an explosion of premium vertical content in the next 18 months,” he said, adding that brands not engaging “will get left behind.”

Others argued that the brand itself should become the content. McDonald’s VP of marketing Elizabeth Campbell and Known president Ross Martin discussed Meal Ticket, the Prime Video documentary tied to the 50th McDonald’s All American Games. Chris Long, CEO of Longshot Productions, the company behind The Beekeeper franchise, said. “If you have the money and means, instead of spending it on a marketing campaign, why not put it in a film where it will live forever?”

Andrew Gottlieb of NBCUniversal’s Rock Studios, the branded content unit NBCU launched at Cannes in June, added the line I’d tape to the monitor of anyone running AI-generated ad variations at scale. “AI can do a lot, and it can create a lot of content, but it can’t make people care about that content.”

Put those together, and the takeaway for PPC teams is uncomfortable. Search and shopping campaigns harvest demand. When brands shift money back to the top of the funnel, the question your CMO will ask is how much of your conversion volume that upper-funnel spend created. If you can’t answer it, someone else will.

See also: How To Measure PPC Performance When AI Controls The Auction

IAB CEO David Cohen gave the line that ties the four signals together. Sitting down on Day 3 with Forbes contributor Howard Homonoff, he said, “The one thing that we simply cannot do is the same thing that we’ve done year-over-year.” Marketers love year-over-year comparisons, he acknowledged, “but if there was a time for a clean sheet of paper and taking advantage of the innovation in the market, it’s now.”

According to festival co-founder William Mellis, as recounted to Net Influencer, Cohen also raised the need for a common currency to measure advertising across fragmented distribution.

I agree with Cohen on the clean sheet. I’d add one condition he didn’t state on stage.

Notice who was making the case against reach in Miami. BBC Studios, YouTube, and Transmit were sponsors, and NBCUniversal and Adelaide sell the alternatives. That doesn’t make them wrong. Sellers often see the shift first because they’re the ones being asked to prove value. But it does mean paid media teams should treat “reach is over” as a hypothesis to test before they budget against it.

Attention scores, affinity grades, and fandom indexes are all better questions than “how many people saw it.” None of them is an answer until you’ve tied it to incremental sales in your own accounts. Ground-truth the new metrics the same way we should have ground-truthed CPM a decade ago.

Here’s how I’d turn the Miami signals into planning moves for a paid media or PPC team this quarter.

1. Add a quality column to every upper-funnel line item. For YouTube, CTV, and programmatic video, report an attention or media quality score next to CPM and view rate. Then run at least one test that compares high-scoring and low-scoring placements on conversion lift, so you know whether the score predicts results in your accounts.

2. Budget for creator content as ad creative. Set aside test money to run creator-made assets through paid formats such as Meta partnership ads, TikTok Spark Ads, or YouTube creator partnerships. Judge them with the same holdouts, bidding strategies, and conversion tracking you use for search, since that discipline is exactly what Tarpey said the market lacks.

3. Reset your year-over-year baseline. If your 2026 numbers include World Cup or midterm-season inventory, flag it before finance compares 2027 against it. Cohen’s advice to stop running the same plan year after year applies to the comparison too.

4. Write the measurement memo before your CMO asks for it. One page that explains how upper-funnel spend feeds your search and shopping conversions, and which test will prove it, is how a PPC manager starts sounding like a director.

Jupiter Festival’s organizers have already put Miami 2027 on the calendar. My bet is that by then, the speakers will have stopped arguing about whether reach is the wrong KPI and started arguing about which replacement is right.

PPC teams that have run their own tests by then will have something worth saying. The rest will be taking notes.

#7410. When hackers become sources: Inside the new craft of reporting on hacked data

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“You’ve definitely seen the maturity of some hackers in how they approach the media. It’s not just about posting things to Twitter like it might have been before.”

Some consequential reporting of recent years has emerged thanks to what is normally defined as a “hack-and-leak,” a specific kind of cyberattack that results in the release of the information obtained by hackers. When Anonymous and allied collectives breached corporations and state agencies during the hacktivist wave of the 2010s, for instance, they turned stolen data into front-page news.

Reporters covering the invasion of Ukraine have frequently worked with documents pulled from Russian institutions by hackers of different allegiances. Hacktivists have breached surveillance vendors and spyware firms, granting journalists direct and exclusive access to the internal files of companies that sell to repressive governments. Ransomware gangs, cybercriminal groups, and state-affiliated hackers deposit fresh troves of hacked data on the open internet, or route it to the public through intermediaries like Distributed Denial of Secrets.

How are journalists responding to these reporting scenarios? For my research, recently published in Journalism Practice, I interviewed 10 journalists across the U.S. and Europe who work or have worked with hacked data. Some of them specialize in the coverage of cyber issues; others mainly focus on current affairs and global conflict. These journalists work for a variety of news outlets, from investigative reporting newsrooms to general interest outlets and technology brands, and have engaged with hacker sources at various levels.

The journalists I spoke with paint a picture of an emerging craft, rather than a settled method. Here’s some of what I found.

There are no fixed guidelines or established and shared practices on how to handle and report on hacked material in news reporting. Instead, the methods are being developed by practitioners on a case by case basis. One reporter who works for an investigative newsroom told me:

Hackers themselves are becoming increasingly strategic about their relationships with the press. One reporter following a specific cyber beat emphasized this:

“I’d say that [hackers] of all kinds love to flex and get credit. A lot of them don’t, but many absolutely do. I’m not sure if the desire to flex has increased, but you’ve definitely seen the maturity of some hackers in how they approach the media. It’s not just about posting things to Twitter like it might have been before.

That maturity means developing awareness of how a story will be framed and disseminated and calculating which journalist to approach. Hackers now may select their outlets of choice, matching a leak to the reporter who they think is capable of understanding the story and carrying it further.

There are different kinds of hackers, wearing different and/or multiple hats. Interviewees drew distinctions between financially motivated cybercriminals, whose leaks are often equivalent to extortion by other means, and state-affiliated actors, who may also pose as independent hacktivists to launder politically motivated leaks into credible coverage.

At the same time, some hackers or hacker collectives — like Phineas Fisher, known for his activist remit against surveillance companies — may act for political and public interest–oriented reasons, reaching out to journalists to expose wrongdoing, unethical issues, or crimes. Notoriously, though, hacking is not a field in which hats are worn straightforwardly: Identities, definitions and agendas, including mere trolling, may blur into one another.

Hacked material needs to be handled with a great deal of skepticism. When working with hacked sources, one journalist said, it’s a matter of “treating every dataset as if it has chlamydia.” But the verification techniques the journalists said they use — such as confirming that an email address exists in a company’s records, cross-referencing with known facts, or examining a file for signs of tampering — are fairly conventional. This type of reporting requires more disclosures, especially when a source’s identity can’t be established. One journalist working in this area said:

I think you should be very transparent about that in your reporting. You should say something like, “We don’t know who the source is; it could be the GRU [Russian Federation] or whoever, but we have confirmed that this data is real and this is what it shows.”

Declared openly, the uncertainty may become a meaningful part of the story itself.

Source protection is further complicated when it comes to hackers. Some interviewees extend the full protection they would give any source to hackers, refusing to assist law enforcement even if the source is a self-declared criminal. Others prefer to know as little as possible about their sources, framing the choice as harm reduction for both parties. As one journalist in my sample put it:

The less I know about these things, the harder it’s going to be for me to burn my source or to publish something that inadvertently turns out to be harmful to my source.

Reporters working exclusively with material already circulating online in cybercrime forums or other repositories on the web treat source protection as beside the point, because the origins of the information cannot be traced and because the material is in effect “out there.”

Beneath all of this sits the finding with the widest implications: Ethical decisions in this domain resist strict codification. No general rule can be written in advance, the reporters I spoke with suggested, and judgment in the individual case is the only workable guide. Is publishing hacked material justified? It depends on the specifics of the case at hand, one reporter told me.

I kind of think it all depends on what you’re exposing. Maybe it’s generally wrong to break into people’s computers and steal data, but if you’re exposing serious crimes, then I think it can be justified.

Interviewees described practical wisdom under pressure: the ability to read a specific situation and act appropriately n it, without having the opportunity to refer to an established code or checklist.

Newsrooms, meanwhile, may need to develop verification standards suited to information of illicit origin, transparency norms that treat uncertainty as something to disclose rather than paper over, and a shared language for the ethical judgments that journalists currently make case by case on their own.

Philip Di Salvo is a senior researcher and lecturer at the Institute for Media and Communications Management at the University of St. Gallen, Switzerland. Adobe Stock

#7409. Two out of five Americans regularly get their news on Facebook

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Despite what my Facebook feed looks like, the platform’s not just for AI fruit videos and birthday posts.

According to data from the Pew Research Center published Monday, 40% of adults in the United States regularly get their news from Facebook.

That’s up from 36% in 2020, signaling the continued stability of the platform as a news source — a trend that the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism observed in its Digital News Report this year. As we reported in June, people around the world are increasingly abandoning news websites for social media.

The Center surveyed 5,600 U.S. adults in late August as part of its American Trends Panel, and asked respondents several questions about their news and social media habits. Pew did not give respondents a definition of “news,” instead letting them use their own understanding of the term when they filled out the survey. More than half (59%) said that they get news from social media “often or sometimes,” but only 19% actually prefer social media as a place to get news.

Of Facebook news consumers, 33% are men and 49% are between the ages of 30 and 49. The platform is most popular for women (47%), Hispanic Americans (51%), Americans with a high school diploma or less (46%), and Republicans (43%).

Regular news consumption among American users has increased on nine of the 12 social media platforms that Pew studied, including YouTube, Instagram, TikTok, X (Twitter), Reddit, Nextdoor, LinkedIn, and WhatsApp. News consumption has either dropped or stayed the same on Rumble, Truth Social, and Bluesky.

The second-most regularly used platform among American adults is YouTube (34%), followed by Instagram (23%), TikTok (20%), and X (10%). YouTube news consumers are more likely to be male (41%), between ages 18 and 29 (39%), and identify as Black (47%) or Asian (53%). Republicans (35%) and Democrats (36%) are equal YouTube news consumers.

The most regularly used platform for news among young adults is Instagram (43%), followed by Facebook (40%), TikTok and YouTube (both 39%), and X and Reddit (both 18%).  The Center found that 20% of U.S. adults now regularly get their news on TikTok, up from 3% in 2020. Of TikTok users, 53% reported getting news regularly on the platform. Nextdoor users are also increasingly turning to the neighborhood forum app for information. In 2026, 45% of Nextdoor users reported regularly getting news from the app, up from 23% in 2022.

AI Mode now links home service searches to booking and quote pages. Here's how businesses reach those pages and what partners say about lead fees.

Google is allowing home service businesses to accept bookings and quote requests generated by AI Mode via Partner Platforms such as the Marketplaces (Angi & Thumbtack) and Field Service Software providers (Housecall Pro & Jobber). On X Wednesday, Google Search Product VP, Robby Stein made a statement regarding the changes and stated that this product is available now in the U.S.

For a plumber or cleaning company, the way in is its field service software or marketplace account. Jobber says its eligible U.S. customers can take those requests now with no lead fees. Housecall Pro also says there are no lead fees, though its release says its integration is coming soon.

Today, we’re making it even easier to research & book home services with direct links in AI Mode through partners like @angi_home @thumbtack @housecall & @GetJobber (and @ServiceTitan coming soon). It’s available now in the U.S.

In the video posted, a searcher is asking to get a handyman to come by and build a bed and dresser the next day. AI Mode identifies local handyman services with online availability along with other service providers who are able to provide a quote. The listing of each service provider includes their rating along with a brief description of what they do. The first of these listings also lists two available times for an appointment.

In May at Google’s I/O conference, Google announced plans to roll out its agentic booking experience to cover additional types of local experiences & services, including direct links to finish booking with the provider. At that same event Google stated that users will be able to ask Google to call businesses for them (in areas such as home repair, beauty & pet care) and that both features would be rolled out nationwide this summer. On Wednesday, Google announced links to named partner companies providing access to booking Home Services.

Jobber announced this week that eligible customers in the United States can be found and booked using AI Mode. According to Jobber’s Help Page, there are certain requirements for businesses to appear in AI Mode. The business must have an active and paid Jobber subscription, a full address listed in Jobber and a Google Business Profile connected to Jobber (listed at the same location), and the business must have assigned a request or booking form to Google, and Jobber defaults to connecting these forms to Google. Trial subscriptions cannot appear in AI Mode.

Once Google identifies a matching profile, a “Book Online” button appears on the business’s Google Business Profile with a link directly to the business’ Jobber booking form. Most times Google will find a match within a few days as stated in the help page.

Requests and bookings made through AI Mode come into Jobber just like another online booking would. There is no lead fee associated with these bookings and they follow the schedule and availability that the business has established. For assessment bookings, they are automatically confirmed by Jobber unless the business has turned on an approval feature that allows them to accept or decline each one individually before it is confirmed. In announcing the integration, Jobber CEO Sam Pillar explained that he believes his company should assist professionals in showing up when customers use AI to search “while keeping ownership of the customer relationships they’ve worked hard to build.”

Housecall Pro states that all of its users will be able to show up in AI Mode at no additional charge. When a Homeowner makes a request, it will be sent to the selected Professional’s Housecall Pro account inbox. Co-Founder & Chief AI Officer of Housecall Pro, Roland Ligtenberg describes it as “One request, one Pro, no lead fee, no bidding war.”

According to Housecall Pro’s Partner page, every one of Housecall Pro’s Professionals are auto-enrolled in AI Mode without having anything to do on their part. The available time slots will be pulled from the Professional’s Calendar, and according to the partner page, no Google Business Profile is required for a Professional to show up in AI Mode. However, the release does say that the integration is coming soon to eligible US Customers.

Angi says homeowners who select an Angi pro that shows up in AI Mode will go straight to that pro’s Angi Profile where they can get more information about the pro and make a quote request. Thumbtack is on Stein’s list however Thumbtack did not announce an AI Mode plan via press releases as of Nov. 4.

For home service businesses, the platform they picked to run jobs or find customers now also affects whether they can take booking and quote requests from Google’s AI search. What it takes to qualify differs by platform, down to whether a Google Business Profile is required.

Jobber’s and Housecall Pro’s no-lead-fee terms contrast with Google’s own Local Services Ads, whose help page lists a customer’s booking request as a lead advertisers are charged for in the U.S. and Canada. Angi’s annual report says pros pay it fees for consumer matches, but its AI Mode announcement doesn’t say whether those fees apply to quote requests that start in AI Mode.

A business cannot rely solely on qualifying for a partner platform to show up; though Stein’s post does not describe how Google determines which businesses to display in AI mode. On the other hand, Jobber’s help page states if a customer collects client reviews and uses a booking form instead of just a request form then that can help have their business recommended by Google AI mode more frequently.

Customers of Jobber can verify whether their Jobber addresses are the same as those entered into their Google Business Profile. Housecall Pro customers should find out whether their account qualifies with Google AI mode, and Angi pros can check their Angi profile, because according to Angi, the profile information on Angi is where Google’s AI mode sends homeowners to choose from.

Stein listed ServiceTitan as coming soon. A business on none of the listed platforms has no route to direct bookings through AI Mode.

Google’s help page on checking local availability in AI Mode, doesn’t mention partner links. For the latest updates, keep an eye on that page and each partner’s eligibility rules.
